questions.question: What is Selenium, and why do we use it?
questions.answer: Selenium is a free, open-source suite of tools for automating web browsers. Its main component, Selenium WebDriver, lets you write code (Java, Python, C#, JavaScript and more) that opens a real browser and performs the same actions a user would: clicking, typing, navigating and reading what is on the page. The suite also includes Selenium Grid for running tests on many machines and browsers in parallel, and Selenium IDE for record-and-playback. We use it because it is free, supports all major browsers and operating systems, works with many languages and test frameworks (TestNG, JUnit, Cucumber), and plugs easily into CI/CD pipelines. Selenium automates only web applications; it cannot automate desktop applications, and mobile apps need Appium.
questions.realTimeExample: An e-commerce team has 400 regression test cases that take three testers four days to run manually before each release. After automating them with Selenium WebDriver and running them on Selenium Grid across Chrome, Firefox and Edge, the same regression completes overnight and the results are waiting in the morning.

questions.question: What are the differences between Selenium 3 and Selenium 4, and which Selenium 4 features have improved your framework?
questions.answer: The biggest change is the protocol. Selenium 3 used the JSON Wire Protocol, which needed encoding and decoding between the client and the browser driver. Selenium 4 uses only the W3C WebDriver standard, so the client talks to the driver directly and behaviour is more consistent across browsers. Other Selenium 4 additions: relative locators (above, below, toLeftOf, toRightOf, near); switchTo().newWindow() to open a new tab or window; element-level screenshots; Chrome DevTools Protocol and BiDi support for network interception, console logs and geolocation; a redesigned Grid that can run as standalone, hub-node or fully distributed with Docker and Kubernetes support; Selenium Manager (from 4.6) which downloads browser drivers automatically; and waits that take a Duration object instead of a long plus TimeUnit. Browser Options classes replace DesiredCapabilities.
questions.realTimeExample: After upgrading, our framework dropped the WebDriverManager dependency because Selenium Manager resolves the driver on its own, replaced a JavaScript window.open() hack with switchTo().newWindow(WindowType.TAB), and started attaching element-level screenshots of the failing component instead of the whole page.

questions.question: What is Selenium WebDriver and its architecture? Is WebDriver an interface or a class?
questions.answer: WebDriver is an interface. It declares browser-control methods such as get(), findElement(), getTitle(), close() and quit(). It extends the SearchContext interface, which is where findElement() and findElements() are declared. RemoteWebDriver is the class that implements WebDriver (and also JavascriptExecutor and TakesScreenshot), and the browser classes ChromeDriver, FirefoxDriver and EdgeDriver extend it. The architecture has four parts: (1) the client library, your Java code; (2) the W3C WebDriver protocol, where each command is sent as an HTTP request with a JSON body; (3) the browser driver (chromedriver, geckodriver, msedgedriver), a small server that receives those requests; and (4) the real browser, which the driver controls natively. The response travels back along the same path.
questions.realTimeExample: When your test calls driver.findElement(By.id("login")).click(), the Java client sends a POST request to chromedriver asking it to find the element, chromedriver asks Chrome and returns an element ID, and a second POST request tells Chrome to click that element. If the element is missing, the driver returns an error that the client turns into NoSuchElementException.

questions.question: What does WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); mean, and why do we prefer it over ChromeDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();?
questions.answer: WebDriver is the interface, driver is the reference variable, new creates the object, and ChromeDriver() is the constructor of the class that implements WebDriver for Chrome. Creating the object starts chromedriver and opens a new Chrome session. Holding a child-class object in a parent-interface reference is called upcasting, and it is an example of runtime polymorphism. We prefer the WebDriver reference because the test code then depends only on the interface, so the same code can run on any browser by changing only the object that is created. With ChromeDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(), the variable is tied to Chrome, and every method that accepts or returns that driver would have to change to support Firefox or Edge. The trade-off is that a WebDriver reference exposes only WebDriver methods, so you cast when you need JavascriptExecutor or TakesScreenshot.
questions.realTimeExample: A driver factory reads the browser name from a config file and returns the matching object. Page classes and tests accept WebDriver, so switching the whole suite from Chrome to Edge is a one-word change in the config file.

questions.question: Can we write RemoteWebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); instead of WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();? Explain the reason.
questions.answer: Yes, it compiles and runs. ChromeDriver extends ChromiumDriver, which extends RemoteWebDriver, so a ChromeDriver object can be held in a RemoteWebDriver reference. RemoteWebDriver is a concrete class that implements WebDriver, JavascriptExecutor and TakesScreenshot, so with this reference you can call executeScript() and getScreenshotAs() without casting. It is still not the usual choice: the code becomes tied to a concrete class rather than the interface, which is weaker design, and it reads as if the test runs on a remote Grid when it does not. The common practice is to declare WebDriver and cast only where the extra capability is needed.
questions.realTimeExample: A utility that takes screenshots receives a WebDriver and casts it: ((TakesScreenshot) driver).getScreenshotAs(OutputType.FILE). The cast works for local drivers and for a RemoteWebDriver pointing at a Grid, so the utility stays browser-independent.
questions.javaCode:
RemoteWebDriver remote = new ChromeDriver();      // valid
remote.executeScript("return document.title;");   // no cast needed

WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();             // preferred
JavascriptExecutor js = (JavascriptExecutor) driver; // cast when required
js.executeScript("return document.title;");

questions.question: What is the use of WebDriverManager?
questions.answer: Every browser needs a matching driver executable (chromedriver, geckodriver, msedgedriver). Originally you had to download the correct version by hand and point to it with System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", path), and tests broke whenever the browser auto-updated. WebDriverManager is an open-source library by Boni Garcia that removes this manual work: it detects the installed browser version, downloads the matching driver, caches it and configures the path. Since Selenium 4.6, Selenium ships its own built-in tool called Selenium Manager that does the same job automatically, so in current projects simply writing new ChromeDriver() is enough and WebDriverManager is optional.
questions.realTimeExample: Chrome on the CI agents updated from one major version to the next over a weekend and every test failed with 'session not created: This version of ChromeDriver only supports Chrome version ...'. After moving to WebDriverManager (and later Selenium Manager) the matching driver is resolved at run time and that failure stopped occurring.

questions.question: What is the role of DesiredCapabilities in Selenium?
questions.answer: Capabilities are key-value pairs that tell the driver or the Grid what kind of session you want: browser name, browser version, platform, whether to accept insecure certificates, and browser-specific settings. DesiredCapabilities was the class used to build them in Selenium 2 and 3. In Selenium 4 it is discouraged in favour of browser-specific Options classes such as ChromeOptions, FirefoxOptions and EdgeOptions, which are type-safe and W3C compliant. The Options classes implement the Capabilities interface, so they can be passed directly to a local driver or to RemoteWebDriver. Cloud providers such as BrowserStack and Sauce Labs take their vendor settings through setCapability() with a vendor prefix, for example "bstack:options".
questions.realTimeExample: To run a test on Selenium Grid against Chrome on Linux, the framework builds ChromeOptions, sets the platform name and passes the options to RemoteWebDriver with the Grid URL. The Grid reads the capabilities and routes the session to a node that matches.

questions.question: What are the limitations of Selenium WebDriver?
questions.answer: Selenium automates only web browsers. Its main limitations are: it cannot automate desktop applications or native operating-system dialogs such as the file-open window; it cannot automate native mobile apps without Appium; it has no built-in reporting, test management or assertions, so you add TestNG or JUnit and Extent or Allure; it cannot reliably automate CAPTCHA, OTP or barcode and image-based verification; it has no built-in image comparison for visual testing; it needs programming skills and there is no official vendor support, only the community; and tests need careful synchronization because Selenium does not automatically wait for dynamic content the way newer tools do. It is also not meant for performance or load testing.
questions.realTimeExample: A registration flow sends an OTP by SMS. Selenium cannot read the phone, so the team either uses a fixed OTP configured for the test environment or fetches the OTP from the database or an API, and then lets Selenium type it in.

questions.question: What is the difference between get() and navigate().to()?
questions.answer: Both load a URL in the current window and both wait for the page to finish loading according to the page-load strategy. In the Java binding, navigate().to(url) simply calls the same underlying command as get(url), so there is no difference in loading behaviour. The real difference is in what else is available: get() only opens a URL and accepts only a String, while navigate() returns a Navigation object that also offers back(), forward() and refresh(), and its to() method accepts either a String or a java.net.URL object. A common wrong answer is that get() waits for the page to load and navigate().to() does not; that is not true.
questions.realTimeExample: A test opens a product list, clicks a product, uses navigate().back() to return to the list and checks that the previously applied filter is still selected, then uses navigate().refresh() to confirm the filter survives a reload.

questions.question: What is the difference between driver.quit() and driver.close()?
questions.answer: close() closes only the browser window or tab that the driver is currently focused on. If other windows are open, the session stays alive and you must switch to another window before continuing. quit() closes every window opened by the session, ends the WebDriver session and stops the driver process (for example chromedriver.exe). After quit() the driver object cannot be used; any call throws NoSuchSessionException. If close() is used on the last remaining window, the browser closes, but always use quit() in teardown, otherwise driver processes can be left running and consume memory on the machine.
questions.realTimeExample: A test clicks a link that opens a help page in a new tab. The test switches to the new tab, verifies the heading, calls close() to shut only that tab, switches back to the main tab and continues. The @AfterMethod then calls quit() to end the session.

questions.question: What are the return types of getWindowHandles() and findElements()?
questions.answer: getWindowHandles() returns Set<String>: one unique handle ID for every window or tab open in the session. getWindowHandle() (singular) returns a single String for the current window. findElements() returns List<WebElement>: all elements matching the locator, in the order they appear in the DOM, or an empty list when nothing matches. findElement() (singular) returns a single WebElement. The collection types follow the data: window handles are unique and have no meaningful index, so a Set is used; elements can be many, are ordered and are accessed by position, so a List is used.
questions.realTimeExample: To count the links in a footer you call findElements(By.cssSelector("footer a")).size(). To confirm that clicking 'Open report' produced exactly one new tab you check that getWindowHandles().size() is 2.

questions.question: How do you run Selenium tests in headless mode?
questions.answer: Headless mode runs the browser without a visible window. The page is still rendered and JavaScript still runs; it is just not drawn on a screen. You enable it through the browser's Options class: for Chrome and Edge add the argument --headless=new, and for Firefox add -headless. Headless runs are common on CI servers and Docker containers that have no display, and they are usually a little faster. Two things to remember: set an explicit window size, because the headless default is small and can trigger the mobile layout and hide elements; and keep taking screenshots on failure, because you cannot watch the run. The older HtmlUnitDriver is a simulated browser, not a real one, and is rarely used now.
questions.realTimeExample: A Jenkins agent running on Linux has no monitor. The framework reads headless=true from the pipeline parameters and adds --headless=new and --window-size=1920,1080 to ChromeOptions, so the same tests that run visibly on a laptop run invisibly in CI.

questions.question: What are the different ways to maximize a browser window in Selenium?
questions.answer: There are four common ways. (1) driver.manage().window().maximize() maximizes after the browser has opened; this is the most used. (2) Add the argument --start-maximized to ChromeOptions so the browser opens already maximized. (3) driver.manage().window().setSize(new Dimension(1920, 1080)) sets an exact size, which is the reliable choice in headless mode where maximize() has no real screen to fill. (4) driver.manage().window().fullscreen() switches to full-screen mode, like pressing F11, which hides the address bar. Using a fixed size gives the most repeatable results, because the layout no longer depends on the monitor of the machine running the test.
questions.realTimeExample: Tests passed on developer laptops but failed in CI because the navigation menu collapsed into a hamburger icon at the smaller default window size. Setting a fixed 1920x1080 size in the driver factory made the layout identical everywhere.

questions.question: How do you run Selenium scripts on an already opened browser?
questions.answer: Normally new ChromeDriver() always starts a fresh browser. To attach to an existing one, Chrome must have been started with remote debugging enabled. Step 1: launch Chrome from the command line with --remote-debugging-port=9222 and a separate --user-data-dir. Step 2: in the script, set the experimental option debuggerAddress to localhost:9222 in ChromeOptions and create the driver. ChromeDriver then connects to that running browser instead of launching a new one, and the script continues from whatever page is open. This is mainly a debugging aid: you can log in or reach a deep page by hand once and re-run only the failing step many times. It is not suitable for regular test runs because tests should start from a clean, known state.
questions.realTimeExample: A failing step sits behind a login with OTP and a five-page wizard. Instead of repeating the whole flow for each attempt, the engineer opens Chrome with the debugging port, reaches the page manually and repeatedly runs a small script that attaches and tries the corrected locator.

questions.question: How do you launch Internet Explorer in Selenium WebDriver?
questions.answer: Classic Internet Explorer needs the IEDriverServer executable and the InternetExplorerDriver class. IE also needs specific settings to work: Protected Mode must be the same (all on or all off) for every security zone, browser zoom must be 100%, and Enhanced Protected Mode should be off. Because Microsoft retired the IE 11 desktop application in June 2022, the current approach for legacy sites is Microsoft Edge in IE mode: you still use InternetExplorerDriver and IEDriverServer, but configure InternetExplorerOptions with attachToEdgeChrome() and the path to msedge.exe. In an interview, mention both the classic setup and the Edge IE-mode replacement.
questions.realTimeExample: A bank's internal loan application only renders correctly in IE. After IE was retired, the automation suite was switched to Edge in IE mode by changing only the options in the driver factory; the page objects and tests stayed the same.

questions.question: What is an Invalid Certificate exception, and how do you handle it?
questions.answer: When a site's SSL/TLS certificate is expired, self-signed or does not match the domain, the browser shows a warning page such as 'Your connection is not private' instead of the application. In Selenium 4 the navigation then fails with InsecureCertificateException, or the test lands on the warning page and cannot find any element. This is common in QA and staging environments that use self-signed certificates. The fix is to tell the browser to accept insecure certificates through the options: setAcceptInsecureCerts(true), which works for Chrome, Firefox and Edge. Use it only for test environments; in production an invalid certificate is a real defect that should be reported, not bypassed.
questions.realTimeExample: The staging server uses a self-signed certificate. Every test failed at the first step because Chrome displayed the privacy error page. Adding setAcceptInsecureCerts(true) in the driver factory for the staging profile fixed it, while the production smoke suite keeps the default so a bad certificate there is caught.

questions.question: What happens if you receive browser notifications during test execution, and how do you deal with them?
questions.answer: Prompts such as 'example.com wants to show notifications', location access or camera access are drawn by the browser itself, not by the web page. They are not part of the DOM, so Selenium cannot locate or click them, and they are not JavaScript alerts, so switchTo().alert() does not work either. If left alone they can cover part of the page and may cause clicks to be intercepted. The solution is to stop them from appearing by configuring the browser before it starts: for Chrome add the --disable-notifications argument, or set the preference profile.default_content_setting_values.notifications to 2 (block) or 1 (allow). For Firefox set the preference dom.webnotifications.enabled to false.
questions.realTimeExample: A news site shows 'Allow notifications?' on every first visit, and because each test starts a clean browser profile the prompt appeared in every test. Blocking notifications in ChromeOptions inside the driver factory removed it for the whole suite.

questions.question: What is the ideal way to store data using Selenium WebDriver only?
questions.answer: Selenium WebDriver has no feature for storing or reading test data; it only drives the browser. So with WebDriver alone, data read from the page is held in the programming language's own structures: Java variables for single values, and collections such as List<String> or Map<String, String> for multiple values, kept for the duration of the test. For data that must live outside the run you combine Selenium with other libraries: properties files for configuration, Excel through Apache POI, JSON through Jackson or Gson, or a database through JDBC. The honest interview answer is to state clearly that data storage is not Selenium's job, then explain where you keep run-time data and where you keep external test data.
questions.realTimeExample: A test captures the order number shown on the confirmation page into a String variable and later searches for the same number on the 'My Orders' page. For a product list, the names and prices of all rows are stored in a Map so they can be compared with the cart.

questions.question: Write the complete steps for navigating to Google in Selenium 4.
questions.answer: The steps are: (1) add the selenium-java dependency to the Maven pom.xml; (2) create the driver object, which starts the browser (in Selenium 4.6 and later, Selenium Manager finds the driver automatically, so no System.setProperty is needed); (3) maximize the window and set any timeouts; (4) call driver.get() with the full URL including https://; (5) verify you reached the right page, for example by checking the title; (6) call driver.quit() in a finally block or an @AfterMethod so the browser always closes, even when the test fails.
questions.realTimeExample: This is the 'hello world' of Selenium and is often asked as a screen-share exercise. Interviewers look for the https:// in the URL, a verification step and quit() in a finally block rather than only opening the page.

questions.question: Automate a login and verify it succeeded, written the way your framework does it: driver and browser setup, parent classes and POM structure.
questions.answer: Show three layers. A BaseTest class owns the driver life cycle: it creates the driver in @BeforeMethod and quits it in @AfterMethod, and test classes extend it (inheritance). A page class per screen holds private locators and public action methods (encapsulation), and receives the driver through its constructor. The test class contains only the business flow and the assertion. Verify success with something that only a logged-in user sees, such as the URL or a page heading, not merely that the click did not fail. Note that real Google sign-in blocks automated browsers, so demonstrate the pattern on your own application or a practice site, and say so in the interview.
questions.realTimeExample: The example below logs in to the public practice site saucedemo.com. The same three classes are how the pattern looks in a real project, only with more page classes and with the URL and credentials read from a configuration file.

questions.question: How would you automate a complete login-to-payment workflow?
questions.answer: Treat it as one end-to-end business flow built from small reusable steps. Use a page object for each screen (Login, Products, Cart, Checkout, Payment, Confirmation), with each action method returning the next page. Keep test data outside the code and use test payment details supplied by the payment gateway's sandbox, never real cards. Add an assertion at each checkpoint: logged-in state, cart contents and total, and finally the order confirmation and order number. Use explicit waits for page transitions. If the payment form sits inside a gateway iframe, switch into the frame first. Handle sandbox OTP or 3-D Secure pages with the fixed codes the sandbox provides. Finish with a back-end check: verify the order through an API or database query, because a confirmation page alone does not prove the payment was recorded. Keep only a few of these long UI tests and cover the variations at API level.
questions.realTimeExample: For an online store, the flow is: log in, add two products, open the cart and assert the total equals the sum of the item prices, enter the shipping address, switch to the gateway iframe and pay with a sandbox test card, assert the 'Order placed' message, capture the order ID, then call GET /orders/{id} and assert the status is PAID and the amount matches.

questions.question: What are the different locators in Selenium? Which one is preferred, which should be avoided, and what is the best approach to locating elements?
questions.answer: Selenium has eight locator strategies, all created through the By class: id, name, className, tagName, linkText, partialLinkText, cssSelector and xpath. Preference order: use id when it is unique and stable, because it is the simplest and most readable; then name; then a dedicated test attribute such as data-testid through a CSS selector; then CSS selectors in general; and XPath when you need something CSS cannot do, such as matching visible text or moving up to a parent. Avoid absolute XPath (starting from /html), because any layout change breaks it; avoid index-based locators and auto-generated ids or classes that change on each build; and be careful with linkText on multi-language sites. className accepts only a single class name, not several separated by spaces. The best approach is to pick the shortest locator that is unique and unlikely to change, and to ask developers to add stable test ids.
questions.realTimeExample: A login button has id='btn-7f3a9' which changes on every deployment. Instead of that id, the team locates it with the stable attribute the developers added: By.cssSelector("[data-testid='login-submit']").

questions.question: What is the difference between findElement() and findElements(), including the exceptions and return values when nothing matches?
questions.answer: findElement() returns a single WebElement, the first match in DOM order. If nothing matches it throws NoSuchElementException (after the implicit wait, if one is set). findElements() returns a List<WebElement> containing every match. If nothing matches it does not throw anything; it returns an empty list, so you check size() or isEmpty(). Use findElement() when the element must exist and its absence should fail the test. Use findElements() when you need several elements (all rows, all links) or when you want to check whether something is present without a try/catch. Neither method returns null.
questions.realTimeExample: To check that an error message is NOT shown after a valid login, use findElements(By.id("error")).isEmpty(). Using findElement() here would throw NoSuchElementException on the correct behaviour and would need a try/catch.

questions.question: If an XPath matches two elements on a page, does findElement() throw an exception?
questions.answer: No. findElement() does not complain about multiple matches; it silently returns the first matching element in DOM order (top to bottom of the HTML). This is risky rather than safe: the first match may not be the element you meant, for example a hidden duplicate, which leads to errors such as ElementNotInteractableException or to the test acting on the wrong element. To target a specific one, make the locator unique by adding a parent or an extra attribute, or use an index on the whole result such as (//button[text()='Login'])[2], or use findElements() and pick from the list. Always confirm in browser DevTools that your locator shows '1 of 1'.
questions.realTimeExample: A page has a 'Search' button in the header and another in the filter panel. //button[text()='Search'] returned the header button, so the filter was never applied and the test failed later with a confusing assertion error. Scoping the locator to the panel, //div[@id='filters']//button[text()='Search'], fixed it.

questions.question: What is the difference between XPath and CSS selectors, and when do you use XPath over CSS?
questions.answer: Both locate elements by their position and attributes, but they differ in power and syntax. CSS selectors are shorter, easier to read and are the browser's native way of selecting elements, so they are generally a little faster. They can only move forward: from parent to child, or to following siblings. XPath can move in any direction, including up to a parent or ancestor and back to preceding siblings, and it can match on visible text with text() and contains(). Use XPath when you need to (1) find an element by its text, (2) go from a child to its parent or ancestor, (3) use a preceding sibling, or (4) combine complex conditions with and/or. Use CSS for everything else, especially id, class and attribute matching.
questions.realTimeExample: In a users table, you know the email 'ravi@test.com' and need the Delete button in the same row. CSS cannot go from the email cell up to the row, but XPath can: //td[text()='ravi@test.com']/parent::tr//button[text()='Delete'].

questions.question: What are the types of XPath (absolute vs relative), and which one is better?
questions.answer: Absolute XPath starts from the root of the document with a single slash and lists every level down to the element, for example /html/body/div[2]/form/input[1]. Relative XPath starts with a double slash and begins from any point in the document, usually identifying the element by its own attributes or text, for example //input[@id='email']. Relative XPath is better. An absolute path breaks as soon as a developer adds, removes or reorders any element along the path, even one unrelated to your element. A relative XPath depends only on the properties you chose, so it is shorter, easier to read and survives layout changes.
questions.realTimeExample: A marketing banner was added at the top of the home page. Every absolute XPath on that page failed because div[2] had become div[3], while the relative locator //input[@id='email'] kept working without any change.

questions.question: What is the difference between a single slash (/) and a double slash (//) in XPath?
questions.answer: A single slash selects the direct child only: one level down from the current node. At the very start of an expression it means 'begin at the document root'. A double slash selects descendants at any depth: children, grandchildren and so on. At the start of an expression it means 'search the whole document'. So //div/a finds links that are immediate children of a div, while //div//a finds links anywhere inside a div, however deeply nested. Use / when the structure is fixed and you want an exact relationship, and // when the nesting level may vary or is not important.
questions.realTimeExample:
For
  • Home
, the expression //div[@id='menu']/a finds nothing because the link is not a direct child of the div, but //div[@id='menu']//a finds the Home link.

questions.question: What are XPath axes (parent, child, ancestor, following-sibling, preceding-sibling)? Give examples of where you use them and the functions you use most.
questions.answer: Axes describe a direction to move from a known element to a related element. They are used when the target has no reliable attribute of its own but sits near something that does. Syntax: axisname::tagname. Main axes: parent (one level up), ancestor (any level up), child (one level down), descendant (any level down), following-sibling (later elements with the same parent), preceding-sibling (earlier elements with the same parent), and following / preceding (anything after or before in the document). The shortcut '..' means parent. Frequently used functions: text() for exact text, contains() for partial text or attribute, starts-with() for a fixed prefix, normalize-space() to ignore extra spaces, last() and position() for indexing, and the operators and / or.
questions.realTimeExample: A form has <label>Email</label><input> with no id on the input. Anchor on the stable label text and move to its sibling: //label[text()='Email']/following-sibling::input. In a table, find the checkbox for a known user: //td[text()='Ravi']/preceding-sibling::td/input[@type='checkbox'].

questions.question: When and why do you use text() in XPath, and how does it differ from contains()?
questions.answer: text() refers to the text node directly inside an element. //button[text()='Login'] matches a button whose own text is exactly 'Login': same case, no extra characters or spaces. Use it when the visible label is the most stable thing about the element and it has no good id or attribute. contains() checks for a partial match and takes two arguments. With text, //button[contains(text(),'Log')] matches 'Login', 'Log in' and 'Logout'. With an attribute, //input[contains(@id,'user')] matches ids such as 'user_123'. So text()= is exact and contains() is partial. Two practical points: text()='Save' fails when the HTML has surrounding spaces or line breaks, so use normalize-space()='Save'; and when the text is split across child tags, use contains(.,'text'), where the dot means the element's full text including its children.
questions.realTimeExample: A success banner reads 'Order #48213 placed successfully'. The number changes every time, so an exact match is impossible; //div[contains(text(),'placed successfully')] locates it reliably.
questions.javaCode:
driver.findElement(By.xpath("//button[text()='Login']"));                 // exact
driver.findElement(By.xpath("//div[contains(text(),'placed successfully')]")); // partial text
driver.findElement(By.xpath("//input[contains(@id,'user')]"));            // partial attribute
driver.findElement(By.xpath("//button[normalize-space()='Save']"));       // ignores extra spaces
driver.findElement(By.xpath("//p[contains(.,'Welcome')]"));               // includes child text

questions.question: What is the syntax for locating a link (linkText locator or XPath for a link)?
questions.answer: Links are <a> tags, and Selenium has two locators made for them. By.linkText("text") matches the complete visible text of the link exactly, and By.partialLinkText("part") matches any part of it. Both work only on <a> elements and are case-sensitive. With XPath you can match the same link by text, //a[text()='Forgot Password?'], by partial text, //a[contains(text(),'Forgot')], or by its href attribute, //a[@href='/forgot-password'] or //a[contains(@href,'forgot')]. The CSS equivalent for href is a[href*='forgot']. Matching on href is often more stable than matching on text, because the visible text changes with wording updates and translations.
questions.realTimeExample: A site is available in English and Hindi. By.linkText("Contact Us") fails on the Hindi version because the label is translated, while By.cssSelector("a[href='/contact']") works in both languages.

questions.question: Write the syntax to find an element through CSS or XPath (for example //input[@id='submit']) and an XPath that identifies a unique element on a page.
questions.answer: Basic XPath syntax is //tagname[@attribute='value']. Basic CSS syntax is tagname[attribute='value'], with shortcuts # for id and . for class. To make a locator unique, add conditions until it matches exactly one element: combine attributes with and, add a parent that is unique, or use stable text. Always verify uniqueness in the browser: open DevTools, press Ctrl+F in the Elements panel and paste the expression; it should show '1 of 1'. In the Console you can also run $x("xpath") for XPath or $$("css") for CSS and check that the returned array has one item.
questions.realTimeExample: A page has two inputs with type='submit', one for search and one for newsletter sign-up. //input[@type='submit'] matches both. Adding a second attribute, //input[@type='submit' and @value='Subscribe'], or a unique parent, //form[@id='newsletter']//input[@type='submit'], makes it unique.

questions.question: What are relative locators in Selenium 4?
questions.answer: Relative locators, originally called friendly locators, find an element by where it is displayed on the page in relation to another element. They are useful when the target has no good attribute but sits next to something that does. There are five methods: above(), below(), toLeftOf(), toRightOf() and near() (within about 50 pixels by default). You start with RelativeLocator.with(By...) describing the target, then chain one or more of these methods. Internally Selenium uses JavaScript's getBoundingClientRect() to compare the positions of elements. Their limitation is that they depend on the visual layout, so a change in window size, responsive design or overlapping elements can change the result; use them as a fallback rather than a first choice.
questions.realTimeExample: A login form has a password field with an id but the 'Show password' checkbox next to it has no usable attribute. It is located as the checkbox to the right of the password field.

questions.question: What is the difference between @FindBy and driver.findElement()?
questions.answer: driver.findElement(By...) searches the page immediately, at the moment the line runs, and returns the element or throws NoSuchElementException. @FindBy is an annotation from Selenium's Page Factory that only declares how a field should be located. When PageFactory.initElements(driver, this) is called, each annotated field receives a proxy object, and the real search happens later, each time the field is used. This is called lazy initialization. Because the lookup is repeated on every use, a @FindBy field picks up a refreshed element automatically, unless you add @CacheLookup, which stores the first result and can then cause StaleElementReferenceException if the page changes. @FindBy keeps page classes concise, but it cannot build locators from run-time values; for dynamic locators you still need By with findElement().
questions.realTimeExample: A page class declares the login button with @FindBy(id = "login"). Creating the page object does not fail even if the button has not rendered yet; the lookup happens only when loginButton.click() runs. A product link whose text is decided at run time is located with By.xpath built from the product name.

questions.question: How do you handle dynamic elements whose IDs or attributes change on every refresh, and what do you do when dynamic XPaths break after a release?
questions.answer: First find what does not change. Options, in order of preference: (1) a stable attribute such as name, data-testid, aria-label, placeholder or type; (2) the fixed part of a changing value, using contains() or starts-with() in XPath, or ^= (starts with), $= (ends with) and *= (contains) in CSS; (3) stable visible text; (4) a stable neighbouring element, reached with XPath axes such as following-sibling or ancestor. Note that ends-with() belongs to XPath 2.0 and browsers support only XPath 1.0, so use the CSS $= operator instead. Add an explicit wait, since dynamic elements often load late. When locators break after a release: confirm the cause in DevTools, fix the locator in one place (which is why locators live in page classes), rerun the affected tests, and for the long term agree with developers on dedicated test ids so the problem does not repeat.
questions.realTimeExample: A submit button's id is 'submit_8421' on one load and 'submit_1077' on the next. The prefix is constant, so it is located with //button[starts-with(@id,'submit_')] or the CSS selector button[id^='submit_'].

questions.question: Open any e-commerce website and write the XPath of the search bar.
questions.answer: The interviewer wants to see your method, not a memorized string. Right-click the search box, choose Inspect and read the attributes of the input tag. Prefer id, then name, then placeholder or aria-label. Write the XPath as //input[@attribute='value'], then press Ctrl+F in the Elements panel and paste it to confirm it shows '1 of 1'. On Amazon the search input has id 'twotabsearchtextbox', so the XPath is //input[@id='twotabsearchtextbox']. On Flipkart the search input has name 'q', so //input[@name='q'] works. Since an id is available on Amazon, By.id is the simplest locator in real code; say that as well. Websites change their HTML, so always verify against the live page rather than quoting from memory.
questions.realTimeExample: During a screen-share round, the candidate inspected Amazon's search box, wrote //input[@id='twotabsearchtextbox'], showed '1 of 1' in DevTools, and then offered a second option using the name attribute, //input[@name='field-keywords'], as a fallback.

questions.question: Write the XPath for the Google Search button.
questions.answer: On the Google home page the 'Google Search' button is an input with name='btnK' and value='Google Search'. The catch is that the page contains two such buttons: one in the main page and one inside the suggestions dropdown, and at any moment one of them is hidden. So //input[@name='btnK'] matches two elements and findElement() returns the first, which may not be the visible one. Safer choices are to index the whole result, (//input[@name='btnK'])[2], or to wait until the button is clickable. In practice most scripts avoid the button entirely: type the query in the search box (name='q') and press ENTER. Google changes its markup from time to time and shows a different layout by region, so confirm the attributes in DevTools.
questions.realTimeExample: A script clicked //input[@name='btnK'] right after typing and failed with ElementNotInteractableException because the suggestion list had covered the main button. Sending Keys.ENTER to the search box made the test stable.

questions.question: Open Airtel.com and write an XPath to retrieve the text of all 11 sliders.
questions.answer: This tests whether you can write one XPath for a repeating group and deal with carousels. Steps: inspect one slide and find the tag and class shared by every slide and by the text element inside it; write an XPath for that common pattern without an index, so it matches all slides; confirm in DevTools that the count is 11; then use findElements() and loop. The trap is that a carousel shows only one or two slides at a time, and getText() returns an empty string for elements that are not visible. Read the text with getAttribute("textContent") instead, which returns it whether or not the slide is displayed. Many carousel libraries also clone the first and last slides for looping, so exclude the clones (often marked with a class such as 'slick-cloned') or you will count more than 11. The actual class names must be taken from the live page.
questions.realTimeExample: If each slide is <div class='slick-slide'> containing an <h2> heading, the XPath is //div[contains(@class,'slick-slide') and not(contains(@class,'slick-cloned'))]//h2. The loop prints 11 headings even though only one slide is visible on screen.

questions.question: Write a dynamic XPath for product ratings on Myntra.
questions.answer: A dynamic XPath here means one expression that works for any product, with the product name passed in at run time. On a Myntra listing page each product is an <li> with class 'product-base'; the name is in an <h4> with class 'product-product' and the rating sits in a <div> with class 'product-ratingsContainer' whose first <span> holds the number. To get the rating of a specific product, anchor on the product name, go up to the product card with the ancestor axis, then come down to the rating. To get all ratings, drop the name condition and use findElements(). Not every product has a rating, so handle the empty case. Class names on live sites change, so verify them in DevTools before relying on them.
questions.realTimeExample: To verify that sorting by 'Customer Rating' works, the test collects every rating on the page with one XPath, converts the text to numbers and asserts that the list is in descending order.

questions.question: Write a dynamic XPath for the 'Check availability' button on Rediffmail.
questions.answer: On the Rediffmail registration page many fields have name attributes with a random suffix that changes on every page load, so an exact match on name or id fails on the next run. The 'Check availability' button is an input of type button whose value is the fixed text 'Check availability'. The stable XPath therefore uses the value attribute: //input[@value='Check availability']. If you prefer the name, match only its constant prefix with starts-with() or contains(), for example //input[starts-with(@name,'btnchkavail')]. The general rule this question tests: when part of an attribute is random, either use a different attribute that is constant or match only the constant part.
questions.realTimeExample: A recorded script used the full generated name and passed once, then failed on every later run with NoSuchElementException. Switching to the value-based XPath fixed it permanently.

questions.question: Write an XPath to locate the 'Senior Citizen' label on the SpiceJet UI.
questions.answer: The SpiceJet booking page is built with a framework that renders almost everything as <div> elements with auto-generated class names such as 'css-76zvg2', and with no ids. Those class names are not reliable, so the dependable property is the visible text. The XPath is //div[text()='Senior Citizen']. If there is surrounding white space use //div[normalize-space()='Senior Citizen'], and if the text might be wrapped in another tag use //*[text()='Senior Citizen']. To click the option, click this label or its clickable parent, reached with /parent::div or /ancestor::div[1], because the radio icon is a separate sibling element. Verify the tag in DevTools, since the site is updated often.
questions.realTimeExample: The test selects the 'Senior Citizen' fare type before searching for flights. Because the framework regenerates class names on each release, a class-based locator broke every few weeks, while the text-based XPath has stayed valid.

questions.question: Two login buttons have the same properties, one in the header and one in the footer. How do you write an XPath for the second one?
questions.answer: There are two reliable ways. (1) Scope by a unique parent: start from the footer container and then find the button inside it, for example //footer//button[text()='Login'] or //div[@id='footer']//button[text()='Login']. This is the better option because it does not depend on order. (2) Index the complete result set: (//button[text()='Login'])[2]. The parentheses are essential. Without them, //button[text()='Login'][2] means 'a Login button that is the second button child of its own parent', which usually matches nothing because each button is the first button inside its own container. With the parentheses, XPath first collects all matching buttons in the whole document and then takes the second.
questions.realTimeExample: The header Login opens a popup and the footer Login navigates to a full login page. The test for the full page uses //footer//button[text()='Login'], so it keeps working even if a third Login button is later added to a sidebar.

questions.question: Write an XPath to locate a specific web-table cell based on the value of a neighbouring cell.
questions.answer: Find the cell you know, then move to the cell you want within the same row. Two patterns are used. (1) Sibling axis: //td[text()='Ravi']/following-sibling::td[2] means 'from the cell containing Ravi, take the second cell to its right'. Use preceding-sibling for cells to the left. (2) Row-first: //tr[td[text()='Ravi']]/td[3] means 'find the row that has a cell with the text Ravi, then take its third cell'. The row-first form is often clearer because the column number is counted from the start of the row and does not depend on where the known cell sits. Remember that XPath indexes start at 1, not 0.
questions.realTimeExample: In an employee table with columns Name, Department, Salary and Action, the test needs Ravi's salary: //tr[td[text()='Ravi']]/td[3]. To click Edit in Ravi's row: //tr[td[text()='Ravi']]//button[text()='Edit'].

questions.question: How do you write XPaths for elements that disappear (for example toast messages or auto-hiding suggestions)?
questions.answer: The difficulty is inspecting something that vanishes before you can look at it. The solution is to freeze the page while the element is visible. Method 1: open DevTools, go to the Console and run setTimeout(() => { debugger; }, 5000), then trigger the element; after five seconds the page pauses and you can inspect it. Method 2: open the Sources tab and press F8 (or Ctrl+\) at the moment the element appears. Method 3: for dropdowns that close when focus is lost, enable 'Emulate a focused page' in the DevTools Rendering panel. Method 4: on the parent element choose 'Break on > subtree modifications'. Once you can see the HTML, write a normal XPath based on class, role or text. In the script, never use a fixed sleep: use an explicit wait for visibility and read the text immediately, because the element will be removed soon after.
questions.realTimeExample: After saving a profile, a toast 'Profile updated' shows for three seconds. Using the debugger trick, the engineer saw it is <div role='alert' class='toast success'>. The test waits for //div[@role='alert'] to be visible, asserts the text and optionally waits for it to become invisible before the next click.

questions.question: What is the difference between implicit and explicit wait? When do you use each, why choose one when both could work, and what is the explicit-wait syntax?
questions.answer: Waits solve the timing gap between the script, which runs instantly, and the page, which loads at its own speed. An implicit wait is a global setting applied once to the driver: every findElement() and findElements() call keeps retrying until the element is present in the DOM or the timeout expires. It checks only presence, not whether the element is visible or clickable. An explicit wait is written for one specific element and one specific condition using WebDriverWait and ExpectedConditions, such as visibility, clickability, text present or an alert being present. It polls every 500 milliseconds by default and throws TimeoutException if the condition is never met. Choose explicit waits as the standard: most failures happen when an element is present but not yet ready, which an implicit wait cannot detect. Do not mix both; the Selenium documentation warns that it causes unpredictable wait times. Neither is Thread.sleep(), which always pauses for the full time.
questions.realTimeExample: After clicking 'Pay', the Confirm button exists in the DOM immediately but stays disabled for two seconds while the total is recalculated. An implicit wait finds it at once and the click does nothing. An explicit wait for elementToBeClickable waits until it is enabled and then clicks.

questions.question: What is Fluent Wait, in which cases is it required, and what is its syntax?
questions.answer: FluentWait is an explicit wait in which you control three things: the maximum time to wait (withTimeout), how often the condition is checked (pollingEvery), and which exceptions to ignore while waiting (ignoring). WebDriverWait is actually a subclass of FluentWait with defaults already set: polling every 500 milliseconds and ignoring NotFoundException. You need FluentWait when the defaults do not fit: when the element appears at irregular intervals and you want a different polling frequency, when you need to ignore additional exceptions such as StaleElementReferenceException, when you want a custom condition written as a lambda, or when the thing you are waiting on is not a WebDriver at all, for example a File in a download folder. It throws TimeoutException if the condition is not satisfied in time.
questions.realTimeExample: A report page shows 'Processing...' and replaces it with a Download link after anywhere between 5 and 60 seconds. A FluentWait with a 60-second timeout, polling every 2 seconds and ignoring NoSuchElementException waits only as long as needed without checking twice every second.

questions.question: How do you use WebDriverWait together with a ThreadLocal driver?
questions.answer: In parallel execution each thread has its own browser, stored in a ThreadLocal<WebDriver> so that threads cannot see each other's driver. A WebDriverWait is bound to the driver passed to its constructor, so it must also be per thread. The mistake to avoid is a single static WebDriverWait shared by all tests: it stays attached to whichever driver created it, so other threads end up waiting on the wrong browser and fail with timeouts or stale-session errors. The correct approaches are to create the wait from the current thread's driver whenever it is needed, for example in a helper method that calls DriverManager.getDriver(), or to keep the wait in its own ThreadLocal next to the driver. Always call remove() on the ThreadLocal during teardown to avoid leaking sessions when threads are reused from a pool.
questions.realTimeExample: A suite ran fine sequentially but failed randomly with thread-count=5. The cause was 'public static WebDriverWait wait' in the base class, created by the first test. Replacing it with a getWait() method that builds the wait from the thread's own driver removed the random failures.

questions.question: How would you wait until the number of browser tabs becomes 4?
questions.answer: New tabs open asynchronously, so reading getWindowHandles() immediately after a click can return the old count. Use an explicit wait with the built-in condition ExpectedConditions.numberOfWindowsToBe(4), which repeatedly checks the number of window handles and returns true when it equals 4, or throws TimeoutException if that never happens. The same check can be written as a lambda: d -> d.getWindowHandles().size() == 4. After the wait succeeds, fetch the handles and switch to the one you need. Never use Thread.sleep() for this, because the time taken to open tabs varies between machines.
questions.realTimeExample: A dashboard has an 'Open all reports' button that opens three reports in separate tabs. The test waits until the window count is 4 (the original plus three), then loops through the handles and verifies each report title.

questions.question: How do you wait for a file download to complete?
questions.answer: Selenium has no command for download progress, because the download happens in the browser, outside the web page. The approach is: (1) configure the browser to save files to a known folder without showing a dialog, using the download.default_directory preference; (2) after clicking the download link, poll that folder with a FluentWait whose input is the folder (a File) rather than the driver; (3) treat the download as complete when the expected file exists, has a size greater than zero, and no temporary files remain. Chrome writes a .crdownload file while downloading and Firefox writes .part. Use a unique folder per test or clear the folder first, so that an old file cannot produce a false pass, and so parallel tests do not collide.
questions.realTimeExample: A test downloads a monthly statement PDF. It waits up to 60 seconds for statement.pdf to appear with no .crdownload file beside it, then asserts the file size is above zero and opens it with a PDF library to check the account number.

questions.question: A login button becomes enabled only after an API call finishes. How do you handle it?
questions.answer: Wait for the result of the API call as the user would see it, not for the call itself and not for a fixed time. The button is already in the DOM, so an implicit wait or a presence check passes too early. Use an explicit wait with ExpectedConditions.elementToBeClickable(), which succeeds only when the element is both displayed and enabled. If the application disables the button in a non-standard way, for example with a CSS class or aria-disabled='true' instead of the disabled attribute, wait for that specific change using attributeToBe() or a small lambda. If a loading spinner is shown during the call, waiting for the spinner to become invisible is another dependable signal. Avoid Thread.sleep(): it slows every run and still fails when the API is slower than the pause.
questions.realTimeExample: On a login page the button stays disabled until a 'check username' API responds. The test types the username, waits for elementToBeClickable on the button, then clicks. On a slow CI network the call takes four seconds instead of one, and the test simply waits longer and still passes.

questions.question: The application loads slowly and causes TimeoutException or page-load flakiness. How do you fix it?
questions.answer: First find out which timeout is failing: the page-load timeout (driver.get() never completes), a script timeout, or an explicit wait on an element. Then apply the matching fix. (1) Replace fixed sleeps and implicit waits with explicit waits on the exact element or state the next step needs. (2) Wait for the application's own signals: loader or spinner invisible, a key element visible, or specific text present. (3) Set realistic timeouts in one central place so they can be raised for slower environments. (4) Change the page-load strategy from the default NORMAL, which waits for every image and third-party script, to EAGER, which continues once the DOM is ready. (5) For single-page applications, wait for elements rather than for document.readyState, because content arrives after the page reports 'complete'. Finally, if the page really is too slow for a user, raise it as a performance defect instead of hiding it with longer waits.
questions.realTimeExample: Tests timed out on driver.get() in CI because a third-party analytics script took 40 seconds to respond. Switching the page-load strategy to EAGER and waiting explicitly for the login form made the tests reliable, and the slow script was reported to the developers.

questions.question: How do you handle flaky web-table pagination with dynamic polling?
questions.answer: Pagination tests are flaky for two reasons: after clicking Next the old rows are still in the DOM for a moment, so the script reads the same page twice; and row elements found before the click become stale once the table re-renders. The fix is to wait for proof that the page actually changed and to find the rows again on every page. Good signals are: the first row from the old page becomes stale (ExpectedConditions.stalenessOf), the page indicator text changes (for example to 'Page 2'), or the first row's text is different from before. Use a FluentWait that ignores StaleElementReferenceException while polling. Stop the loop when the Next button is disabled or absent, not after a fixed number of clicks. When the data comes from an API, checking the total through the API is faster than paging through the UI.
questions.realTimeExample: A test searching for an order across 12 pages sometimes reported 'not found' even though the order was on page 7. It was reading page 6 twice because the rows had not refreshed. Waiting for the old first row to go stale after each Next click made every page read correctly.

questions.question: How do you handle dropdowns? Write the syntax of the Select class and explain its methods.
questions.answer: For a standard HTML dropdown built with the <select> tag, Selenium provides the Select class in org.openqa.selenium.support.ui. You create it by passing the dropdown element to its constructor. Selection methods: selectByVisibleText(text) chooses by the text the user sees, selectByValue(value) by the option's value attribute, and selectByIndex(index) by position starting from 0. Reading methods: getOptions() returns all options as a List<WebElement>, getFirstSelectedOption() returns the currently selected option, and getAllSelectedOptions() returns every selected option in a multi-select. isMultiple() tells you whether multiple selection is allowed. The deselect methods (deselectAll, deselectByVisibleText, deselectByValue, deselectByIndex) work only on multi-select lists. If the element is not a <select> tag, the constructor throws UnexpectedTagNameException.
questions.realTimeExample: On a registration form the Country dropdown is a <select>. The test chooses 'India' by visible text and then asserts that getFirstSelectedOption().getText() equals 'India' to confirm the selection was applied.

questions.question: How do you select a value from a custom or dynamic dropdown that has no <select> tag (that is, without the Select class)?
questions.answer: Modern frameworks such as React, Angular and Bootstrap build dropdowns from <div>, <ul> and <li> elements, so the Select class cannot be used. Handle them the way a user does. Step 1: click the dropdown control to open it. Step 2: wait explicitly for the options to become visible, because they are often added to the DOM only after the click. Step 3: click the option you want, either with a direct XPath on its text or by collecting all options with findElements() and looping until the text matches. For auto-suggest dropdowns, type part of the value first, wait for the suggestion list and then click the matching suggestion. If the list is long and virtualized, scroll the option into view or type to filter. Finally, assert that the control now displays the chosen value.
questions.realTimeExample: On a travel site the 'From' field is an auto-suggest box. The test types 'Ben', waits for the suggestion list, loops through the suggestions and clicks the one whose text is 'Bengaluru'.

questions.question: How do you get all available values from a dropdown, and how do you capture one value to reuse in later verifications?
questions.answer: For a <select> dropdown, getOptions() returns every option as a List<WebElement>. Loop over the list, or use a stream, and call getText() on each to build a List<String> of the values. To capture the value currently selected, call getFirstSelectedOption().getText() and store it in a String variable. That variable can then be used in later assertions, for example to check that the same value is shown on a summary page. Store the text, not the WebElement: if the page reloads or navigates, the stored element reference becomes stale and using it throws StaleElementReferenceException, while a String remains valid.
questions.realTimeExample: On a checkout page the user picks a delivery slot. The test stores the selected slot text, completes the order, and on the confirmation page asserts that the displayed delivery slot equals the stored value.

questions.question: Write a code snippet to handle multiple selections from a dropdown.
questions.answer: A multi-select list is a <select> element with the multiple attribute. First confirm it with isMultiple(). Then call the select methods repeatedly: each call adds to the selection instead of replacing it. getAllSelectedOptions() returns everything currently selected, and deselectAll() or the individual deselect methods remove selections. Calling a deselect method on a single-select dropdown throws UnsupportedOperationException. For custom multi-select widgets that are not <select> elements, hold the CONTROL key with the Actions class and click each option, or simply click each checkbox-style option in turn.
questions.realTimeExample: A job portal lets a candidate choose several skills from a list. The test selects 'Java', 'Selenium' and 'SQL', asserts that three options are selected, then deselects 'SQL' and asserts that two remain.

questions.question: In a 'District Name' dropdown, how would you verify whether the list is sorted?
questions.answer: Read the actual order, build the expected order by sorting a copy, and compare the two. Steps: (1) get all options with getOptions() and collect their text into a list; (2) remove the placeholder such as 'Select District', which is not part of the data; (3) copy the list and sort the copy with Collections.sort(); (4) assert that the original list equals the sorted copy. Lists are equal only when they hold the same items in the same order, so the assertion fails if the dropdown is unsorted. Decide on case sensitivity first: default sorting puts capital letters before lower-case letters, so use String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER if the requirement is alphabetical regardless of case. For descending order, sort the copy with Collections.reverseOrder().
questions.realTimeExample: The requirement states that districts must appear alphabetically. The test found the actual list was [Mysuru, Bengaluru, Hubballi], compared it with the sorted copy [Bengaluru, Hubballi, Mysuru], and failed with a clear message showing both lists, which was attached to the defect.

questions.question: How do you handle JavaScript alerts and confirmation dialogs, and how do you enter text in an alert?
questions.answer: JavaScript has three kinds of dialogs: an alert (a message with OK), a confirm (OK and Cancel) and a prompt (a text box with OK and Cancel). They are created by the browser, not by HTML, so you cannot inspect or locate them. Selenium handles them through the Alert interface: driver.switchTo().alert() returns the open dialog. Its four methods are accept() to click OK, dismiss() to click Cancel, getText() to read the message, and sendKeys(text) to type into a prompt. Wait for the dialog first with ExpectedConditions.alertIsPresent(); switching when no dialog is open throws NoAlertPresentException. While a dialog is open, any other driver command fails with UnhandledAlertException, so it must be handled before continuing. Pop-ups built from HTML (modal divs) are not alerts and are handled like normal elements.
questions.realTimeExample: Clicking 'Delete account' shows a confirm dialog 'Are you sure?'. The negative test dismisses it and asserts the account still exists; the positive test accepts it and asserts the 'Account deleted' message. A 'Rename' button opens a prompt, where the test types the new name with sendKeys and accepts.

questions.question: A JS alert appears randomly when some button is clicked and you cannot predict when. How do you make sure Selenium accepts it automatically?
questions.answer: The cleanest solution is a browser capability. Set the unhandled prompt behaviour to ACCEPT in the options: options.setUnhandledPromptBehaviour(UnexpectedAlertBehaviour.ACCEPT). The driver then accepts any unexpected alert automatically and the script continues. The W3C default is 'dismiss and notify', which closes the alert but still throws UnhandledAlertException, so setting ACCEPT explicitly is what removes the failure. Other values are DISMISS, ACCEPT_AND_NOTIFY, DISMISS_AND_NOTIFY and IGNORE. A second approach, when you need to log or verify the alert text, is a small helper that checks for an alert with a very short wait and accepts it, called from your common click wrapper, or a try/catch for UnhandledAlertException that handles the alert and retries the step. Also report the random alert to the team: unpredictable behaviour is often a defect in itself.
questions.realTimeExample: A legacy application occasionally shows 'Session about to expire' as a JavaScript alert at any step. Setting the capability to ACCEPT in the driver factory meant no test needed special handling, and the nightly run stopped failing at random steps.

questions.question: How do you handle authentication pop-ups in Selenium?
questions.answer: A basic-authentication pop-up asking for a username and password is drawn by the browser in response to an HTTP 401 status with a WWW-Authenticate header. It is neither HTML nor a JavaScript alert, so findElement() and switchTo().alert() do not work on it. There are two standard solutions. (1) Put the credentials in the URL: https://username:password@host/path. The browser sends them and the pop-up never appears. It is simple, but special characters in the password must be URL-encoded and the password is visible in the code and logs. (2) In Selenium 4 with Chromium browsers, use the HasAuthentication interface: register the credentials once and the browser supplies them whenever a site asks. Tools such as AutoIt or the Robot class also work but are operating-system dependent and fail in headless and Grid runs, so treat them as a last resort.
questions.realTimeExample: The staging site is protected by basic authentication at the web server so the public cannot see it. The driver factory registers the staging credentials with HasAuthentication, read from a secret store, and every test then opens staging pages without seeing the pop-up.
questions.expectedOutput: Congratulations! You must have the proper credentials.

questions.question: How do you handle unexpected pop-ups, modal overlays, cookie-consent banners and pop-ups that appear only on the first visit?
questions.answer: First identify what kind of pop-up it is, because each kind is handled differently: a JavaScript alert needs switchTo().alert(); a browser permission prompt is disabled through browser options; an HTML modal, overlay or cookie banner is ordinary page content and is closed by clicking its button. For HTML pop-ups that may or may not appear, never use findElement() directly, because it fails the test when the pop-up is absent. Use findElements() and act only if the list is not empty, or use a short explicit wait inside a try/catch. Put this check in one reusable method and call it at the points where the pop-up can appear, such as right after opening the site. A cleaner option for cookie banners and first-visit pop-ups is to prevent them: add the consent cookie or local-storage flag that the site sets after acceptance, then refresh. If an overlay blocks a click, wait for it to become invisible before clicking.
questions.realTimeExample: A retail site shows a cookie banner on first visit and sometimes a 'Get 10% off' newsletter modal. The base page has dismissPopupsIfPresent(), called after navigation, which closes whichever of the two is present and does nothing otherwise, so tests pass whether or not the marketing team enables the modal.

questions.question: How do you handle frames and iframes: switching into nested (including multi-domain) frames, returning to the parent, and the different ways to identify a frame?
questions.answer: An iframe is a separate HTML document embedded inside the page. Selenium sees only one document at a time, so you must switch into a frame before locating elements inside it; otherwise you get NoSuchElementException. There are three ways to switch: by index, switchTo().frame(0); by name or id, switchTo().frame("payment"); and by WebElement, switchTo().frame(driver.findElement(...)), which is the most reliable. The best practice is the explicit wait ExpectedConditions.frameToBeAvailableAndSwitchToIt(), which waits for the frame to load and switches in one step. For nested frames switch one level at a time from the outside in; you cannot jump straight to an inner frame. To come back, switchTo().parentFrame() moves up one level and switchTo().defaultContent() returns to the main page. To move between two sibling frames, return to the parent first. Frames from another domain are handled in exactly the same way; the browser's same-origin restriction applies to page JavaScript, not to WebDriver.
questions.realTimeExample: A checkout page embeds the payment gateway in an iframe, and inside it the card-number field is in a second iframe from the bank's domain. The test switches into the gateway frame, then into the card frame, types the card number, calls parentFrame() to reach the Pay button in the gateway frame, and finally defaultContent() to read the order status on the main page.

questions.question: How do you determine whether an element is inside an iframe?
questions.answer: There are several quick checks. (1) In DevTools, select the element and look at the breadcrumb bar at the bottom of the Elements panel, or scroll up through its ancestors: if you pass an <iframe> or <frame> tag and a '#document' node, the element is inside a frame. (2) Right-click on that part of the page: browsers show options such as 'View frame source' or 'Reload frame' only when you click inside a frame. (3) In the DevTools Console, the context dropdown that normally says 'top' lists the available frames. (4) A strong hint during scripting: your locator shows '1 of 1' in DevTools but the script throws NoSuchElementException. (5) In code, driver.findElements(By.tagName("iframe")).size() tells you how many frames the current document contains, and you can loop through them to find which one holds the element.
questions.realTimeExample: A script could not find the 'Card number' field although the XPath was correct in DevTools. Right-clicking the field showed 'View frame source', which confirmed it was inside the payment iframe. Adding a frame switch before the lookup fixed the script.

questions.question: There are three frames (A, B, C). Clicking in Frame C opens a new tab containing login, password and sign-in. Write the Selenium script for this scenario.
questions.answer: Clarify the structure first: are the frames nested (C inside B inside A) or side by side? The script below assumes nested frames; for sibling frames you would switch to defaultContent() and directly into C. The logic is: (1) save the parent window handle; (2) switch into the frames one level at a time, A then B then C; (3) click the element in C; (4) wait until two windows exist; (5) switch to the new window handle. A new tab is a new top-level document, so no frame switching is needed there unless the login form is itself in a frame; (6) fill in the login form and sign in; (7) close the new tab if required, switch back to the parent handle and call defaultContent(), because returning to the original window does not guarantee which frame you are in.
questions.realTimeExample: An internal portal embeds a partner widget in nested frames, and its 'Open partner console' button launches the partner's login page in a new tab. The test below covers exactly that flow and then returns to the portal.
buzzWords: New Tab Is a New Document

questions.question: How do you handle multiple windows or tabs? Write code (with waits) to switch to a child window, perform operations and switch back to the parent.
questions.answer: Selenium identifies each window or tab by a unique string called a window handle. When a link opens a new window, the driver's focus stays on the original one, so you must switch explicitly. Steps: (1) store the parent handle with getWindowHandle() before the click; (2) perform the click; (3) wait until the number of windows has increased, using ExpectedConditions.numberOfWindowsToBe(); (4) get all handles with getWindowHandles(), loop through them and switch to the one that is not the parent; (5) wait for an element or the title on the child, then do the work; (6) call close() to close only the child; (7) switch back to the parent handle. Step 7 is essential: after closing the child, the driver still points to the closed window, and the next command throws NoSuchWindowException.
questions.realTimeExample: On a banking site, clicking 'View statement' opens the statement in a new tab. The test switches to it, verifies the account number, closes the tab and continues on the original accounts page.

questions.question: What is the difference between getWindowHandle() and getWindowHandles()?
questions.answer: getWindowHandle() returns a String: the unique handle of the single window or tab the driver is currently focused on. getWindowHandles() returns a Set<String>: the handles of all windows and tabs opened in the current session, including the current one. A handle is a random identifier generated for the session, for example 'CDwindow-A1B2...'; it is not the page title or the URL, and it is different on every run. The usual pattern uses both: save the parent with getWindowHandle() before opening a new window, then call getWindowHandles() and switch to whichever handle is not the parent.
questions.realTimeExample: Before clicking a 'Terms and Conditions' link that opens a new tab, the test stores getWindowHandle(). Afterwards getWindowHandles() returns two handles, and the one that does not equal the stored value is the new tab.

questions.question: Why is a Set used for window handles?
questions.answer: Because the data matches what a Set represents. Every window handle is unique within a session, and a Set by definition cannot contain duplicates, so the return type itself guarantees that no window is listed twice. Windows also have no meaningful position: the WebDriver specification does not define any order for the handles, so offering index-based access through a List would wrongly suggest that 'index 1' is always the second window. In Selenium's Java binding the returned object is a LinkedHashSet, so in practice the handles usually come back in the order the windows were opened, and many people copy them into an ArrayList to use get(index). That works in common cases but is not guaranteed, so the robust approach is to identify the new window by excluding the known parent handle or by checking the title or URL after switching.
questions.realTimeExample: A test that used new ArrayList<>(driver.getWindowHandles()).get(1) to reach a popup worked locally but picked the wrong window on another browser. Switching by 'handle not equal to parent' and then confirming the title made it reliable on all browsers.

questions.question: How do you close specifically the second open browser tab?
questions.answer: Selenium can only close the window it is focused on, so the steps are: get all handles, switch to the second tab, call close(), then switch back to a tab that is still open. Copy the handles into a List to pick the second by index (index 1), which follows opening order in practice; if the tab can be recognized by its title or URL, switching by that is safer. Use close(), not quit(): quit() would end the whole session and close every tab. The step people forget is switching back afterwards. After close(), the driver still refers to the closed tab, and any further command throws NoSuchWindowException until you switch to a valid handle.
questions.realTimeExample: A test opens three tabs: the dashboard, a report and a help page. The report tab is no longer needed, so the test closes that second tab and continues working with the dashboard and help tabs.

questions.question: How do you open a new tab in Selenium?
questions.answer: In Selenium 4 use driver.switchTo().newWindow(WindowType.TAB). It opens a blank new tab and moves the driver's focus to it automatically, so the next driver.get() loads in the new tab. WindowType.WINDOW opens a separate browser window in the same way. Both belong to the same session, so cookies and login state are shared. Before Selenium 4 the options were JavaScript, ((JavascriptExecutor) driver).executeScript("window.open()"), after which you had to switch to the new handle yourself, or sending CONTROL + T through the keyboard, which is unreliable because the browser's own shortcuts are not part of the web page. Keep the original handle if you need to return to the first tab.
questions.realTimeExample: A test places an order as a customer in one tab, opens a second tab for the admin portal to approve the order, then switches back to the first tab and verifies that the status changed to 'Approved'.

questions.question: How do you manage multi-tab window switching in headless Chrome?
questions.answer: The API is the same as in headed mode: window handles, switchTo().window() and switchTo().newWindow() all work, because headless Chrome still creates separate page targets even though nothing is drawn on screen. What changes is the environment, so apply these practices. Use the new headless mode (--headless=new), which behaves like the normal browser. Set an explicit window size, since each headless tab otherwise uses a small default viewport and may render the mobile layout. Always wait for the window count to change before switching, because CI machines are slower and the timing differs from a laptop. Some sites treat window.open() as a blocked pop-up in headless runs; if no new handle appears, allow pop-ups through the options. Identify the tab by title or URL after switching rather than by index, and capture a screenshot per tab on failure because you cannot watch the run.
questions.realTimeExample: A test that opened an invoice in a new tab passed locally but failed in Jenkins with 'no such window'.
