In headless CI the tab took longer to open and the script switched before the handle existed. Adding numberOfWindowsToBe(2) and a fixed window size fixed the pipeline run.

questions.question: What is the Actions class? Name a few of its methods, and how does it differ from the Select class?
questions.answer: The Actions class (org.openqa.selenium.interactions.Actions) performs advanced user gestures with the mouse and keyboard that a simple click() or sendKeys() cannot. You create it with the driver, chain the steps, and finish with perform(), which actually executes them; build() is optional because perform() builds internally. Mouse methods: moveToElement() for hover, click(), doubleClick(), contextClick() for right-click, clickAndHold(), release() and dragAndDrop(). Keyboard methods: keyDown(), keyUp() and sendKeys(). Selenium 4 added scrollToElement() and scrollByAmount(). The Select class is unrelated in purpose: it works only with HTML <select> dropdowns and offers methods to choose and read options. In short, Actions simulates gestures on any element, while Select is a helper for one specific element type.
questions.realTimeExample: A site's main menu shows the 'Electronics' sub-menu only on mouse hover. The test uses Actions.moveToElement() on the menu, then clicks 'Laptops' in the sub-menu. On the same page a 'Sort by' <select> dropdown is handled with the Select class.

questions.question: How do you perform mouse actions: hover, right-click and drag-and-drop? Write the code.
questions.answer: All three use the Actions class and must end with perform(). Hover: moveToElement(element) moves the pointer to the middle of the element, which triggers hover menus and tooltips. Right-click: contextClick(element) opens the context menu. Drag-and-drop: dragAndDrop(source, target) presses on the source, moves to the target and releases. When that single method does not work, which is common with HTML5 or JavaScript drag libraries, do it step by step with clickAndHold(source), moveToElement(target) and release(), sometimes adding a small moveByOffset() so the page registers the movement. After each action, wait for and assert the visible result, such as the sub-menu appearing or the item being present in the target.
questions.realTimeExample: On a task board, a card is dragged from the 'To Do' column to 'Done'. The test performs the drag and then asserts that the card is now a child of the Done column and that the To Do count dropped by one.

questions.question: How do you perform keyboard actions with the Actions class: Ctrl+A, pressing ENTER, and holding SHIFT to type uppercase? Write the syntax.
questions.answer: Use keyDown() to press and hold a modifier key, sendKeys() to type while it is held, and keyUp() to release it. Ctrl+A is keyDown(Keys.CONTROL), sendKeys("a"), keyUp(Keys.CONTROL). ENTER is a single key press: sendKeys(Keys.ENTER). For uppercase, hold SHIFT with keyDown(Keys.SHIFT) while sending lower-case text to an element, then release it. Always release a modifier with keyUp(), otherwise it stays pressed for later actions. A shorter form for combinations on one element is element.sendKeys(Keys.chord(Keys.CONTROL, "a")). On macOS the equivalent of CONTROL for select-all, copy and paste is Keys.COMMAND, so cross-platform frameworks choose the key based on the operating system.
questions.realTimeExample: To replace the text in a pre-filled field that ignores clear(), the test clicks the field, presses Ctrl+A to select everything, types the new value over it and presses ENTER to submit the search.

questions.question: How do you handle drag-and-drop on an HTML canvas?
questions.answer: A <canvas> is a single element that draws pixels; the shapes inside it are not DOM elements, so there is nothing to locate as source or target. You therefore work with coordinates. Locate the canvas, then use Actions with offsets: moveToElement(canvas, xOffset, yOffset) to reach the start point, clickAndHold(), moveByOffset(dx, dy) to drag, and release(). In Selenium 4 the offsets in moveToElement are measured from the centre of the element, not the top-left corner, which is a frequent source of mistakes. Calculate offsets from the canvas size (getSize()) rather than hard-coding pixels, so the test survives different window sizes. Verification is the harder part: the canvas content cannot be read as text, so assert through something the application exposes, such as a value shown elsewhere in the DOM, application state read through JavaScript, or a screenshot comparison.
questions.realTimeExample: In a signature pad, the test draws a line across the canvas by dragging from the left area to the right area, then asserts that the 'Clear' button became enabled and that the hidden input holding the signature data is no longer empty.

questions.question: How do you hover over SVG graph elements and capture dynamic tooltips?
questions.answer: There are two parts. Locating: SVG elements belong to a different XML namespace, so a normal XPath such as //svg//rect finds nothing. Use the name() or local-name() function: //*[name()='svg']//*[name()='rect']. CSS selectors do not have this problem, so By.cssSelector("svg rect") works directly and is simpler. Hovering: use Actions.moveToElement() on the bar or point, because the tooltip is created only on mouse hover. Then wait explicitly for the tooltip element to be visible and read its text. The tooltip is usually one shared element whose text changes, so read it immediately after each hover, before moving to the next shape. If a shape is very thin, moving to its centre may miss it; add a small offset or use the element's location.
questions.realTimeExample: A sales dashboard shows monthly revenue as an SVG bar chart. The test hovers over each bar, reads the tooltip such as 'March: 4,20,000' and compares the values with the figures returned by the reporting API.

questions.question: Print all customer-salary values from a given graph using Selenium.
questions.answer: First find where the graph keeps its values, because that decides the approach. (1) If each bar or point shows its value in a tooltip on hover, locate all the bars, hover over each with Actions, wait for the tooltip and collect the text. (2) If the values are already in the DOM, as data labels (<text> elements inside the SVG) or as attributes such as aria-label or data-value, read them directly with findElements(); this is faster and more stable than hovering. (3) If the graph is drawn on a <canvas>, the values are not in the DOM at all; read them from the chart's data through JavaScript or from the API that feeds the chart. Store the values in a List, or a Map of customer to salary, so they can be printed and compared with the expected data.
questions.realTimeExample: A bar chart shows the salary of ten customers. Each bar has an aria-label like 'Ravi, 55000'. The test reads the attribute from every bar, splits it and prints each customer with their salary, then asserts the list matches the database query result.

questions.question: What is the Selenium syntax for copying and pasting an image?
questions.answer: Selenium has no dedicated copy-image command, and it cannot use the browser's right-click 'Copy image' option because that menu is native to the browser, not part of the page. Copy and paste is done with keyboard shortcuts through the Actions class: Ctrl+C on the selected content and Ctrl+V in the target (COMMAND instead of CONTROL on macOS). This works when the image can be selected inside the page, for example inside a rich-text editor. When you need to paste an image file from disk, place it on the operating-system clipboard using Java's AWT Toolkit and then send Ctrl+V to the target field. Clipboard-based tests need a real desktop session, so they are unreliable in headless mode and on remote Grid nodes; where the application offers a file-upload input, sending the file path to it is the more dependable route.
questions.realTimeExample: A chat application lets users paste screenshots into the message box. The test loads a PNG onto the system clipboard, clicks the message box, presses Ctrl+V and asserts that an image preview thumbnail appears before sending.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Robot class in Selenium?
questions.answer: Robot is not part of Selenium; it is a Java class (java.awt.Robot) that generates real keyboard and mouse events at operating-system level. It is used alongside Selenium for things outside the browser's web page that WebDriver cannot reach: native file-upload and download dialogs, print dialogs, browser-level pop-ups and pressing system keys. Typical methods are keyPress(), keyRelease(), mouseMove(), mousePress(), mouseRelease() and delay(). Its limitations are important: it acts on whatever window currently has focus, so the browser must be visible and in the foreground; it works with screen coordinates, so it is sensitive to resolution; it cannot read anything back to verify; and it does not work in headless mode or on a remote Grid node, because the events fire on the machine running the Java code. For these reasons it is a last resort after WebDriver-level solutions.
questions.realTimeExample: Clicking 'Print invoice' opens the operating system's print dialog, which Selenium cannot see. The test uses Robot to press ESCAPE and close the dialog so the browser is usable again.

questions.question: What is JavaScriptExecutor? When do you use it, and what can you do with it (scroll, click, set values, fetch text)? Show code.
questions.answer: JavascriptExecutor is a Selenium interface that runs JavaScript inside the browser page. The driver classes implement it, so you cast the driver: JavascriptExecutor js = (JavascriptExecutor) driver. It has two methods: executeScript() for normal scripts and executeAsyncScript() for scripts that finish later through a callback. Elements are passed in as arguments and read inside the script as arguments[0], arguments[1], and a value comes back to Java when the script uses return. Use it when standard WebDriver commands cannot do the job: scrolling, clicking an element that normal click cannot reach, setting a value on a stubborn field, reading values such as document.readyState or the page's inner text, highlighting elements for debugging, and working with browser storage. Use it carefully: JavaScript acts directly on the DOM and does not behave like a real user, so it can pass on something a user could never do. Prefer normal WebDriver actions first.
questions.realTimeExample: A date field is read-only and filled only by a calendar widget. To set many dates quickly in a data-driven test, the script sets the value with JavaScript and fires a change event so the application notices the new value.

questions.question: How do you click hidden DOM elements using JavascriptExecutor?
questions.answer: A normal WebElement.click() refuses to click an element that is not displayed and throws ElementNotInteractableException, because a real user could not click it either. JavaScript does not check visibility: js.executeScript("arguments[0].click();", element) calls the element's click handler directly, even when the element is hidden by display:none, has zero size or is covered. The element only needs to exist in the DOM, so locate it with a presence check rather than a visibility check. Explain the risk in the interview: by forcing the click you may hide a real defect, because the test passes on something a user cannot do. So first ask why it is hidden. If a user would reveal it by hovering, expanding a menu or scrolling, do that instead. Reserve the JavaScript click for genuine cases, such as a visually hidden native checkbox or file input that is replaced by a styled label.
questions.realTimeExample: A custom-styled checkbox hides the real <input type='checkbox'> with CSS and shows a decorative span. Normal click on the input fails as not interactable. Clicking the visible label is the user-like fix; the JavaScript click on the input is the fallback when the label has no stable locator.

questions.question: How do you scroll in Selenium: by pixels (for example 2000 px), to a specific element, and until the footer is visible?
questions.answer: WebDriver scrolls an element into view automatically before clicking it, so explicit scrolling is needed mainly for lazy-loaded content, screenshots and elements hidden under sticky headers. With JavascriptExecutor: window.scrollBy(0, 2000) scrolls down 2000 pixels from the current position (a negative value scrolls up); window.scrollTo(0, document.body.scrollHeight) jumps to the bottom of the page; and arguments[0].scrollIntoView(true) scrolls until a given element, such as the footer, is in view. Using {block: 'center'} places the element in the middle of the screen, which avoids sticky headers covering it. Selenium 4 also has native Actions methods: scrollByAmount(x, y) and scrollToElement(element). A third option is keyboard keys such as Keys.PAGE_DOWN or Keys.END. scrollBy is relative to the current position, while scrollTo uses an absolute position.
questions.realTimeExample: A long landing page loads its footer links only when the footer comes into view. The test scrolls the footer element into view, waits for the links to be visible and then verifies the 'Privacy Policy' link.

questions.question: How do you automate infinite-scroll or lazy-loaded tables and assert on rows?
questions.answer: With infinite scroll, rows are added only as the user scrolls, so the rows present at first are just the first batch. The approach is a loop: count the rows, scroll to the last row or to the bottom, wait for the row count to increase, and repeat. Stop when the count does not change after a scroll (no more data), when an 'end of results' marker appears, or when the row you need is found. Always include a maximum number of scrolls so a defect cannot cause an endless loop. Wait for the count to change instead of sleeping. One special case: virtualized tables keep only the visible rows in the DOM and remove the ones scrolled past, so the DOM count never grows; there, collect each row's unique text or id into a Set while scrolling. For exact total counts, comparing with the API response is more efficient than scrolling thousands of rows.
questions.realTimeExample: An order-history page loads 20 orders per scroll. The test scrolls until no new rows appear, ends with 87 rows, and asserts that the count equals the 'total' field from the orders API and that order ORD-48213 is among them.

questions.question: What are the different ways to click a button or web element in Selenium?
questions.answer: There are five common ways. (1) WebElement.click(): the standard method; it checks the element is visible and enabled and scrolls it into view, so it behaves most like a real user. (2) Actions: new Actions(driver).moveToElement(element).click().perform(), which moves the pointer first and helps when a hover is needed or the click must land at a specific position. (3) JavascriptExecutor: executeScript("arguments[0].click();", element), which triggers the click directly in the DOM and works on hidden or covered elements, but does not imitate a user. (4) submit(): called on a form or any field inside it, it submits the form without clicking the button; it works only for real HTML forms. (5) Keyboard: element.sendKeys(Keys.ENTER) or Keys.SPACE on the focused button. Use them in that order of preference, and before moving to a fallback, find out why the normal click failed.
questions.realTimeExample: A 'Submit' button was covered by a sticky chat widget in a small window, so click() raised ElementClickInterceptedException. Instead of jumping straight to a JavaScript click, the team scrolled the button to the centre of the screen and the standard click worked.
questions.javaCode:
WebElement button = driver.findElement(By.id("login"));

button.click();                                                        // 1. standard

new Actions(driver).moveToElement(button).click().perform();          // 2. Actions

((JavascriptExecutor) driver).executeScript("arguments[0].click();", button);  // 3. JavaScript

driver.findElement(By.id("password")).submit();                        // 4. submit the form

button.sendKeys(Keys.ENTER);                                           // 5. keyboard

questions.question: What are the different ways to enter text into a field (sendKeys() and alternatives)?
questions.answer: (1) WebElement.sendKeys("text"): the standard way; it types key by key and fires the keyboard events that the page listens for. It appends to existing text, so call clear() first when the field may already contain a value. (2) Actions: new Actions(driver).sendKeys(element, "text").perform(), or click the field and send keys to the focused element, useful for fields that need focus or key combinations. (3) JavascriptExecutor: set the value property directly with arguments[0].value = 'text'. This is fast and works on read-only fields, but it fires no keyboard events, so applications built with React or Angular may not register the change unless you also dispatch an 'input' or 'change' event. (4) Clipboard paste: put the text on the clipboard and send Ctrl+V, occasionally needed for very long text. (5) The Robot class, at operating-system level, as a last resort. sendKeys() should be the default because it is closest to real typing.
questions.realTimeExample: A test typed a 5,000-character description with sendKeys() and took 20 seconds on that step. For that single large field the team set the value through JavaScript and dispatched an input event, while every other field continued to use sendKeys().

questions.question: sendKeys() is not entering text even though the locator and code are correct. What could be the reasons?
questions.answer: Work through the likely causes. (1) The locator matches more than one element and the first match is a hidden duplicate, or it matches a wrapper <div> or <label> instead of the actual <input>. (2) The field is inside an iframe or a shadow DOM and the script has not switched into it. (3) Timing: the field is present but not yet enabled or visible, or the framework re-renders the field right after typing and wipes the value. (4) The field is disabled or read-only. (5) An overlay, loader or pop-up is covering the field. (6) The field needs focus first, so a click before typing is required. (7) It is a special input: type='file' needs a file path, type='date' needs the format the browser expects, and masked or auto-formatted fields may reject fast typing. (8) JavaScript on the page handles key events and blocks or reformats input. (9) The browser window has lost focus, which affects some key events. To diagnose, check the count of matches in DevTools, read back getAttribute("value") after typing, take a screenshot at that step and check isDisplayed() and isEnabled().
questions.realTimeExample: A script typed a username and the field stayed empty with no error. DevTools showed the locator matched two inputs: a hidden one in a mobile layout and the visible desktop one. sendKeys() was going to the hidden input. Making the locator unique fixed it.

questions.question: What is ElementClickInterceptedException (element not clickable though the locator is right), and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: It means Selenium found the element and tried to click it, but another element was on top at the click point and would have received the click instead. The error message names the blocking element ('Other element would receive the click: ...'), which is the best clue. Common blockers are a loading spinner or overlay, a cookie banner, a modal, a sticky header or footer, a chat widget, or an animation that is still moving the element. Fixes, matched to the cause: wait for the overlay or loader to become invisible; close the banner or pop-up first; scroll the element to the centre of the viewport so sticky bars do not cover it; wait for elementToBeClickable; maximize or set a larger window size. A JavaScript click will get past it, but it is a last resort because a real user would also be blocked, so forcing it can hide a genuine defect. Do not confuse this with ElementNotInteractableException, where the element itself is hidden or has no size.
questions.realTimeExample: Clicking 'Place order' failed in CI with 'Other element would receive the click: <div class="loader">'. The page showed a loader while prices refreshed. Waiting for the loader to disappear before clicking removed the failure permanently.
buzzWords: Other Element Would Receive the Click

questions.question: How do you fetch the text from a text box, and how do you fetch an element's attribute value?
questions.answer: getText() returns the visible text between an element's opening and closing tags, which works for labels, headings, paragraphs and buttons. A text box (<input> or <textarea>) keeps what the user typed in its value property, not between tags, so getText() returns an empty string. Use element.getAttribute("value") to read it. For any other attribute, pass its name: getAttribute("href"), getAttribute("placeholder"), getAttribute("class"); it returns null when the attribute does not exist. Selenium 4 also offers two more precise methods: getDomAttribute(name) returns the attribute exactly as written in the HTML, and getDomProperty(name) returns the current live property. The difference shows for value: the HTML attribute holds the initial value, while the property holds what is in the box now. getAttribute("value") returns the current value, which is why it is the usual choice.
questions.realTimeExample: After clicking 'Use my saved address', the form auto-fills. The test verifies it with getAttribute("value") on the City field; getText() would have returned an empty string and the assertion would have failed wrongly.

questions.question: Write Selenium code to automate a calendar or date-picker element.
questions.answer: Check the simplest option first: if the date field accepts typing, send the date in the expected format with sendKeys() and you are done. If it is a click-only widget, automate it the way a user would: (1) click the field to open the calendar; (2) read the month and year shown in the header; (3) click Next (or Previous) until the header matches the target month and year; (4) click the target day. When clicking the day, exclude the greyed-out days of the neighbouring months that share the same number, usually through a class such as 'disabled' or 'other-month'. Write this as one reusable method that takes day, month and year, keep a limit on the loop so it cannot run forever, and afterwards assert the field's value. For a past date, decide the direction by comparing the dates.
questions.realTimeExample: On a flight-booking page the departure date must be chosen from a calendar. The test calls selectDate("15", "March", "2027"), which opens the picker, moves forward month by month to 'March 2027' and clicks 15, then asserts the field shows 15/03/2027.

questions.question: How do you interact with dynamic web tables, including ones with sticky headers?
questions.answer: A dynamic table has rows, and sometimes columns, that change with the data, so never hard-code row or column numbers. Read the structure at run time: get the rows with findElements() on tbody tr and the cells of each row with findElements() on td. Find a column by its header name: read the header texts, get the index of the column you want, and use that index for the cells. This keeps the test working when columns are reordered or added. Find a row by a unique value, such as an order id, then act on other cells in the same row. Re-locate rows after any sort, filter or page change, because old references go stale. For sticky headers, the header stays fixed while rows scroll beneath it, so a row scrolled 'into view' can still be covered and the click is intercepted. Scroll the row to the centre of the viewport before clicking. If the header row is duplicated for the sticky effect, locate headers from one specific header element to avoid counting them twice.
questions.realTimeExample: In an orders table the 'Status' column moved from fourth to fifth position after a release. Tests that used td[4] failed, while tests that looked up the index of the 'Status' header kept passing.

questions.question: A particular text can appear in any cell of a web table. How do you locate it dynamically?
questions.answer: Do not include a row or column number in the locator. Search every cell by its text: //table[@id='orders']//td[normalize-space()='Pending'] for an exact match, or contains(., 'Pending') for a partial match. If the text can occur more than once, use findElements() to get all matching cells. To learn where it was found, calculate the position with XPath's count() function: the column number is count(preceding-sibling::td) + 1 on the cell, and the row number is count(preceding-sibling::tr) + 1 on its parent row. From the found cell you can also move to related cells with axes, for example parent::tr to reach the whole row. The same result can be achieved in Java with two nested loops over rows and cells, which is easier to read and lets you print the coordinates.
questions.realTimeExample: A seat-allocation grid shows a passenger's name in whichever seat was assigned. The test searches all cells for 'Asha Rao', then reports the row and column so it can assert she was given a window seat (column 1 or 6).

questions.question: A web table has 3 columns and 4 rows. Sort the second column and get the value of the fourth row.
questions.answer: Clarify which is meant, because there are two readings. Reading 1, sort in code: collect the second-column values from all four rows with the locator //table//tbody/tr/td[2], put them in a List, sort the list with Collections.sort(), and take the fourth item, which is index 3 because lists start at 0. If the values are numbers, convert them to Integer or Double before sorting; sorted as text, '100' comes before '25'. Reading 2, sort in the UI: click the second column's header so the application sorts the table, wait for the table to refresh, then read the second cell of the fourth row with //table//tbody/tr[4]/td[2]. A good test combines both: sort in the UI, read the column again and assert that it equals the list sorted in code, which proves the sort feature works.
questions.realTimeExample: A table lists Name, Salary and City for four employees with salaries 45000, 30000, 60000 and 52000. Sorted ascending, the fourth value is 60000. The test clicks the Salary header and asserts the fourth row shows 60000 and that the whole column matches the sorted list.
questions.expectedOutput:
Sorted: [30000, 45000, 52000, 60000]
Fourth value: 60000
Fourth row after UI sort: 60000

questions.question: How do you locate and handle elements inside a Shadow DOM (open mode), and why do applications use it?
questions.answer: Shadow DOM is a browser feature that attaches a hidden, separate DOM tree to an element, called the shadow host. Applications use it to build web components whose internal HTML and CSS are encapsulated: page styles cannot leak in and component styles cannot leak out, which makes components reusable. The same isolation means normal locators cannot see inside: driver.findElement() stops at the shadow boundary and throws NoSuchElementException. In Selenium 4, locate the host element normally, call getShadowRoot() on it, which returns a SearchContext, and call findElement() on that. Inside a shadow root you must use CSS selectors; XPath is not supported there. For nested shadow roots, repeat the step for each level. Before Selenium 4 the same was done with JavaScript: return arguments[0].shadowRoot. This works only for open shadow roots. A closed shadow root returns null and cannot be reached this way; you then need help from the developers or keyboard navigation. In DevTools a shadow tree appears under '#shadow-root (open)'.
questions.realTimeExample: A design-system login component <app-login> keeps its username input inside an open shadow root. The script first failed with NoSuchElementException on By.id("username"). Locating the host and going through getShadowRoot() solved it.

questions.question: What causes StaleElementReferenceException, and how do you handle it (for example on dynamic React dropdown lists, or after a page refresh)?
questions.answer: When Selenium finds an element it keeps a reference to that exact node in the DOM. The exception is thrown when you use the reference after the node has been removed or replaced: the element is 'stale'. Causes: the page was refreshed or navigated; JavaScript or an AJAX call re-rendered that part of the page; or a framework such as React or Angular rebuilt the list, which it does on almost every state change. The new element may look identical and have the same locator, but it is a different node. The fix is always to locate the element again, never to keep using the old reference. Good practices: store By locators rather than WebElements and find the element just before using it; after an action that refreshes the page, find elements afresh; in loops over a list that re-renders, re-fetch the list inside the loop by index; use ExpectedConditions.refreshed() or a wait that ignores StaleElementReferenceException; and as a safety net, a small retry that re-locates and repeats the action. Avoid @CacheLookup on elements that change.
questions.realTimeExample: A React dropdown filters its options as the user types. The script fetched the option list, typed another letter and clicked the first stored option, which failed as stale because React had rebuilt the list. Re-locating the option after typing, with a wait, fixed it.
buzzWords: Reference No Longer Attached to the DOM

questions.question: Which Selenium exceptions have you faced (give five), and how did you resolve them?
questions.answer: (1) NoSuchElementException: the locator found nothing. Causes are a wrong locator, the element not yet loaded, or the element being inside a frame or shadow DOM. Fix: verify the locator, add an explicit wait, switch into the frame. (2) StaleElementReferenceException: the element was found earlier but the DOM has since been rebuilt. Fix: locate it again just before use. (3) ElementClickInterceptedException: another element such as a loader or banner covers the target. Fix: wait for the overlay to disappear or scroll the element to the centre. (4) ElementNotInteractableException: the element exists but is hidden, disabled or has no size. Fix: wait for visibility, or perform the user step that reveals it. (5) TimeoutException: an explicit wait's condition was not met in time. Fix: check that the condition and locator are right before increasing the timeout. Others worth naming: NoSuchFrameException and NoSuchWindowException from wrong switching, NoAlertPresentException when no alert is open, SessionNotCreatedException from a browser and driver version mismatch, and InvalidSelectorException from a syntax error in the XPath or CSS.
questions.realTimeExample: After a browser auto-update, the whole suite failed at start-up with SessionNotCreatedException saying the driver supported only the previous Chrome version. Moving to Selenium Manager, which picks the matching driver automatically, removed the problem.

questions.question: How do you handle exceptions in Selenium scripts?
questions.answer: The first principle is prevention: most Selenium exceptions are timing problems, and proper explicit waits remove them without any try/catch. Use try/catch only where the situation is expected and recoverable, for example an optional pop-up that may or may not appear, or a retry after a stale element. Never wrap test steps in an empty catch block: swallowing the exception makes a broken test report as passed. When you do catch, either recover, or log the context and rethrow so the test still fails. Put handling in one place rather than in every test: wrapper methods for click and type that include waits and a limited retry, and a TestNG listener (ITestListener.onTestFailure) that takes a screenshot and logs the error for every failure. Use finally or @AfterMethod(alwaysRun = true) to quit the browser so a failure does not leave sessions open. Add a clear message to waits and assertions so the report states what was expected.
questions.realTimeExample: A framework's click() wrapper waits for the element to be clickable and retries once on StaleElementReferenceException. Any other exception is logged with the locator and rethrown, the listener attaches a screenshot to the report, and the browser is closed in @AfterMethod.

questions.question: How do you take screenshots in Selenium: full viewport, full page and a single web element? Write the code.
questions.answer: Viewport (the visible part of the page): cast the driver to TakesScreenshot and call getScreenshotAs(OutputType.FILE), then copy the temporary file to your own location; OutputType.BASE64 and BYTES are useful for embedding the image in reports. Single element: WebElement itself has getScreenshotAs() since Selenium 4, which captures only that element. Full page (including the part below the fold): there is no single cross-browser method. Firefox has getFullPageScreenshotAs() on FirefoxDriver. For Chrome and Edge, use the Chrome DevTools Protocol command Page.captureScreenshot with captureBeyondViewport set to true, or a library such as AShot that scrolls and stitches the page. Give each file a unique name, typically the test name plus a timestamp, so that screenshots are not overwritten in parallel runs.
questions.realTimeExample: On every test failure, the framework's listener saves a viewport screenshot named after the test and timestamp and attaches it to the Extent report. For a visual check of a price badge, an element screenshot is compared against a stored baseline image.

questions.question: How do you handle file uploads (browse button): sendKeys, AutoIt and the Robot class?
questions.answer: The preferred way never opens the operating-system file dialog. Find the <input type='file'> element and call sendKeys() with the absolute path of the file; the browser attaches the file as if the user had chosen it. Do not click the Browse button first, because that opens the native dialog, which Selenium cannot control. The file input is often hidden behind a styled button; sendKeys() still works on many hidden inputs, and if it does not, make the input visible with JavaScript first. When running on a remote Grid, call setFileDetector(new LocalFileDetector()) on the RemoteWebDriver so the file is transferred from your machine to the node. Only when the page has no file input at all (rare, for example some Flash-era or fully custom uploaders) do you fall back to OS-level tools: AutoIt, a Windows-only scripting tool whose compiled .exe types the path into the dialog and is started with Runtime.getRuntime().exec(); or the Robot class, which pastes the path from the clipboard and presses ENTER. Both need a visible desktop and fail in headless and Grid runs.
questions.realTimeExample: A KYC page has a styled 'Upload PAN card' button with a hidden file input. The test sends the file path to the input, waits for the file name 'pan.png' to appear beside the button and then submits the form. No dialog ever opens, so the test also runs headless in CI.
buzzWords: Do Not Open the Native Dialog

questions.question: How do you automate and verify file downloads, including in headless Chrome, and validate the contents of the downloaded file?
questions.answer: Step 1, configure: set Chrome preferences so files save to a known folder with no prompt: download.default_directory, download.prompt_for_download = false, and plugins.always_open_pdf_externally = true so PDFs are downloaded instead of opened in the viewer. With --headless=new, downloads work with these same preferences; the old headless mode blocked downloads unless you sent the CDP command Browser.setDownloadBehavior. Step 2, trigger and wait: click the link and poll the folder until the file exists with no temporary .crdownload file. Step 3, verify the file: check its name, extension and that its size is greater than zero. Step 4, validate the contents with the right library: read CSV or text with java.nio Files, Excel with Apache POI, PDF text with Apache PDFBox, and JSON with Jackson, then assert the expected values. Use a unique download folder per test and clean it afterwards. On a remote Grid the file is saved on the node, so use Selenium 4's managed downloads (the se:downloadsEnabled capability) to fetch it. If only the content matters, calling the download URL through an API client is faster than using the browser.
questions.realTimeExample: A test downloads an orders report as CSV in headless Chrome on Jenkins, waits for orders.csv, then reads the file and asserts that the header row is 'OrderId,Customer,Amount' and that the row count matches the number of orders shown on the page.

questions.question: How do you print all links on a page (and where do you store them), and how do you find broken versus working links? Write the program.
questions.answer: All links are tags, so collect them with driver.findElements(By.tagName("a")) and read each one's href attribute. Store the URLs, not the WebElements, in a collection: a List if duplicates matter, or a Set to check each unique URL once. Skip values that are null or empty and those starting with 'javascript:', 'mailto:' or 'tel:', because they are not web pages. Selenium cannot read HTTP status codes, so the checking is done in Java: for each URL open an HttpURLConnection, send a HEAD request (it returns only the status line and headers, so it is faster than GET), and read the response code. A code of 400 or above means the link is broken, for example 404 Not Found or 500 Server Error; below 400 is working. Set connect and read timeouts, and treat an exception such as an unknown host as broken. Some servers reject HEAD with 405; retry those with GET. The same approach applies to images using the src attribute of tags.
questions.realTimeExample: Before each release, a scheduled job crawls the home page footer and header links. It reported that the 'Careers' link returned 404 after the careers page was moved, and the defect was fixed before customers saw it.

questions.question: How do you capture network logs in Selenium?
questions.answer: Selenium 3 could not see network traffic without an external proxy. Selenium 4 gives three options. (1) Chrome DevTools Protocol: for Chromium browsers, call getDevTools() on the driver, create a session, enable the Network domain and add listeners for events such as requestWillBeSent and responseReceived to record URLs, methods, status codes and timings. The CDP classes are versioned per browser release (for example org.openqa.selenium.devtools.v131), so the import must match your Selenium and browser versions. (2) WebDriver BiDi: the newer cross-browser standard that is replacing CDP in Selenium; it offers network events and interception without version-specific classes. (3) Performance logs: enable LogType.PERFORMANCE through logging preferences and read the entries from driver.manage().logs(), which contain the same network events as JSON. A proxy such as BrowserMob Proxy is the older approach and can export a HAR file. Typical uses are asserting that an API call was made, that no request returned 4xx or 5xx, or that an analytics request fired.
questions.realTimeExample: After clicking 'Add to cart', the UI showed success but orders were sometimes missing. The test was extended to capture network responses and assert that POST /api/cart returned 200; it revealed occasional 500 responses that the UI was hiding.

questions.question: How do you capture browser console errors during a Selenium run?
questions.answer: The browser console holds JavaScript errors and failed resource loads that often explain a failure the UI does not show. For Chromium browsers, enable browser logging in the options with a LoggingPreferences object set on the 'goog:loggingPrefs' capability, then read the entries with driver.manage().logs().get(LogType.BROWSER). Each LogEntry has a level, a timestamp and a message; filter for Level.SEVERE to get errors. Reading the log clears the buffer, so each call returns only what was logged since the previous call, which makes it convenient to read once at the end of each test. This Logs API is not supported by Firefox; for cross-browser capture, and for live events, use Selenium 4's BiDi or DevTools log listeners. In a framework, do this in an @AfterMethod or listener: attach the console errors to the report for failed tests, and optionally fail the test when unexpected SEVERE errors appear, with an allow-list for known noise such as a missing favicon.
questions.realTimeExample: A checkout test failed with a timeout waiting for the 'Pay' button. The console log attached to the report showed 'TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading price)', which pointed the developer straight to the broken script.

questions.question: How do you validate CSS properties such as colour, font and element position?
questions.answer: Use WebElement.getCssValue(propertyName), which returns the computed style: the final value the browser applied after all style sheets. Colour: getCssValue("color") or "background-color" returns the value in rgb or rgba form, for example 'rgba(255, 0, 0, 1)', and the exact format differs between browsers. To compare reliably, convert it with Selenium's Color class: Color.fromString(value).asHex() gives '#ff0000'. Font: read "font-size" (returned in pixels, such as '16px'), "font-family" and "font-weight" (often numeric: 700 for bold). Use the long property names; shorthand such as 'font' or 'border' may return an empty string. Position and size: getLocation() gives the x and y of the top-left corner, getSize() gives width and height, and getRect() gives all four. Exact coordinates change with window size, so fix the window size first and prefer relative checks, such as one element being to the left of or above another. For broad look-and-feel checks, visual comparison tools are better suited than many individual CSS assertions.
questions.realTimeExample: The requirement says a validation error must appear in red (#d32f2f), 14px, directly below the email field. The test asserts the hex colour, the font size and that the error's y coordinate is greater than the field's y coordinate.

questions.question: Can CAPTCHA be automated or validated with Selenium? If so, how?
questions.answer: No, and it should not be. CAPTCHA exists specifically to tell humans from automated scripts, so if Selenium could solve it reliably, the CAPTCHA would be defective. Trying to defeat it with OCR or solving services is unreliable and usually against the site's terms. The correct answer is to handle it through the test environment rather than through the script. Options: (1) ask developers to disable CAPTCHA in QA and staging through a configuration flag; (2) use the provider's official test keys, for example Google reCAPTCHA publishes test keys that always pass; (3) configure a fixed, known CAPTCHA value or a bypass token or header for the automation user in test environments; (4) whitelist the test machines' IP addresses; (5) for a one-off run, pause the script and let a person solve it, which is semi-automated. What you can automate is everything around it: that the CAPTCHA widget is displayed, that the form cannot be submitted without it, and that the back end rejects a missing or invalid token, which is best tested at API level. The same reasoning applies to OTP.
questions.realTimeExample: The registration page uses reCAPTCHA. In staging the team configured Google's test site key, so the widget shows 'testing purposes only' and always passes; the automation simply clicks the checkbox inside the reCAPTCHA iframe. Production keeps the real keys, and production smoke tests skip registration.

questions.question: How do you validate that Google Analytics or Comscore tags are present on a page?
questions.answer: A tracking tag has three observable parts, and you can check each. (1) The script is included: search the DOM for the tag's script element. Google Analytics and Tag Manager load from googletagmanager.com (gtag/js or gtm.js) or the older google-analytics.com/analytics.js; Comscore loads from scorecardresearch.com. Use findElements() on script[src*='...'] and assert the list is not empty, or check that the page source contains the measurement id, such as 'G-XXXXXXX'. (2) The tracking objects exist: with JavascriptExecutor, check that window.dataLayer is defined and has entries, or that typeof gtag is 'function'; for Comscore, that window._comscore or window.COMSCORE exists. (3) The tracking request is actually sent, which is the strongest proof: capture network traffic with Selenium 4 DevTools or a proxy and assert that a request went to google-analytics.com with '/collect' in the path, carrying the expected measurement id and event name, or to b.scorecardresearch.com for Comscore. Wait for the page to finish loading first, because tags usually fire after load, and remember that consent banners can block tags until the user accepts.
questions.realTimeExample: After a site redesign, marketing reported that page views had dropped to zero. The automated tag check then caught the cause in the next build: the Tag Manager script was missing from the new page template, so no analytics request was being sent.

questions.question: What is Selenium Grid, and what are its advantages?
questions.answer: Selenium Grid is the part of Selenium that runs tests on other machines instead of the machine where the test code is. The test sends its commands to one central address, and the Grid forwards them to a machine, called a node, that has the requested browser. In the test, the only change is to create a RemoteWebDriver with the Grid URL instead of a local driver such as ChromeDriver. Advantages: (1) parallel execution, many tests run at the same time on several nodes, which cuts total run time; (2) cross-browser and cross-platform coverage, the same tests run on Chrome, Firefox and Edge on Windows, Linux and macOS; (3) central management, browsers are installed and maintained on the nodes, not on every tester's machine; (4) scalability, add nodes or Docker containers as the suite grows; (5) easy use from CI/CD pipelines. Grid does not make a single test faster and does not create parallelism by itself; the test runner (TestNG or JUnit) starts the parallel threads and the Grid supplies the browsers.
questions.realTimeExample: A regression suite of 600 tests took 5 hours on one machine. Using a Grid with 10 Chrome nodes and TestNG running 10 threads, the same suite finishes in about 35 minutes, and a nightly job repeats it on Firefox and Edge.

questions.question: How does Selenium Grid work in the latest version (router, distributor, session map, event bus: the async architecture)?
questions.answer: Grid 3 had two parts, a hub and nodes, and the hub was a single bottleneck. Grid 4 was rewritten into six components that can run together or separately. The Router is the single entry point that receives every request. The New Session Queue holds new-session requests in order until a browser slot is free. The Distributor knows every node and its free slots; it takes a request from the queue and picks a node whose capabilities match. The Node runs the browsers and executes commands. The Session Map stores which node owns each session id. The Event Bus is the messaging channel through which the components notify each other, for example 'node added' or 'session created', instead of calling each other directly; this is what makes the design asynchronous. Flow for a new session: Router, then Queue, then Distributor, which asks a Node to start the browser and records the session in the Session Map. Flow for every later command: the Router looks up the session id in the Session Map and forwards the command straight to that Node, without involving the Distributor. Grid 4 runs in three modes: standalone (everything in one process), hub and node, or fully distributed with each component as its own process, which suits Docker and Kubernetes.
questions.realTimeExample: When 50 tests start at once against a Grid with 20 free slots, 20 sessions are created immediately and the other 30 requests wait in the New Session Queue rather than failing. As tests finish and slots are released, the Distributor serves the queued requests in order.

questions.question: How would you design a Selenium Grid for parallel execution, and how do you execute tests on a remote machine?
questions.answer: Start from the numbers: how many tests, how long they take, and the target run time decide how many parallel sessions are needed. Each browser session needs roughly one CPU core and 1 to 2 GB of memory, so size the nodes accordingly rather than overloading them, which causes slow and flaky tests. For the platform, the common design is Docker: the official selenium/hub and selenium/node-chrome, node-firefox and node-edge images, started with Docker Compose for a fixed size, or on Kubernetes with autoscaling so nodes are created on demand and removed after the run. Clean containers per run also avoid leftover browser state. Set sensible session timeouts so abandoned sessions are freed, and enable video or VNC for debugging. For browsers or devices that are hard to host, use a cloud grid such as BrowserStack or Sauce Labs. On the test side, to run remotely: read the Grid URL and browser from configuration, create a RemoteWebDriver with the URL and browser options, keep the driver in a ThreadLocal, set a LocalFileDetector for uploads, and let TestNG provide the threads. Keep a 'local' switch so the same tests can run on a developer machine.
questions.realTimeExample: A team needs 1,200 tests in under 30 minutes. At about 1 minute per test they need roughly 40 parallel sessions, so the pipeline starts a Kubernetes Grid that scales to 40 Chrome pods, runs TestNG with thread-count 40, publishes the report and scales the Grid back to zero.

questions.question: How do you run tests in parallel in Selenium, and what challenges have you faced doing so?
questions.answer: Selenium itself does not run tests in parallel; the test runner does. With TestNG, set parallel and thread-count on the <suite> tag in testng.xml: parallel='methods' runs test methods in separate threads, 'classes' runs each class in its own thread, and 'tests' runs each <test> block in its own thread, which is the usual choice for cross-browser runs. A DataProvider can run in parallel with @DataProvider(parallel = true). Each thread needs its own browser, kept in a ThreadLocal, and Selenium Grid or a cloud grid supplies enough browsers. Challenges: (1) a shared static WebDriver causes threads to drive each other's browser; fix with ThreadLocal. (2) Shared test data, such as two tests using the same user or editing the same record; fix with unique data per test. (3) Tests that depend on execution order; make each test independent. (4) Shared files, such as one download folder or one report object; use per-thread folders and thread-safe reporting. (5) Too many threads for the machine, which makes tests slow and timing-sensitive; match the thread count to the hardware. (6) Hidden shared state in static variables and singletons.
questions.realTimeExample: When a suite was switched to five threads, tests began logging in as the wrong user and clicking on the wrong pages. The base class held 'static WebDriver driver', so all threads shared the last browser created. Moving the driver into a ThreadLocal fixed it.
questions.javaCode:
<!-- testng.xml -->
<suite name="Regression" parallel="methods" thread-count="5">
    <test name="All tests">
        <classes>
            <class name="tests.LoginTest"/>
            <class name="tests.CartTest"/>
            <class name="tests.CheckoutTest"/>
        </classes>
    </test>
</suite>

// Parallel data-driven test
@DataProvider(name = "users", parallel = true)
public Object[][] users() {
    return new Object[][]{{"user1"}, {"user2"}, {"user3"}};
}

questions.question: How do you make a framework thread-safe for parallel runs (ThreadLocal WebDriver initialization, no data leakage), and how would you fix a framework that is not thread-safe?
questions.answer: Thread-safe means every test thread works only with its own objects. The core is ThreadLocal<WebDriver>: a container that stores a separate value for each thread, so getDriver() in one thread never returns another thread's browser. Initialize the driver in @BeforeMethod with set(), use it through a static getDriver(), and in @AfterMethod call quit() followed by remove(). remove() matters because threads come from a pool and are reused; without it the next test can receive a dead driver, and sessions leak. To fix a framework that is not thread-safe, audit for shared mutable state and remove it step by step: (1) replace 'static WebDriver driver' with a ThreadLocal-based DriverManager; (2) make page objects per test, created with the thread's driver, never static or cached; (3) remove static variables that hold test data or state, or make them ThreadLocal too; (4) make utilities stateless; (5) use thread-safe reporting, for example a ThreadLocal<ExtentTest>; (6) give each thread unique test data and its own download folder; (7) replace HashMap with ConcurrentHashMap where a shared map is truly needed. Then prove it by running with a high thread count repeatedly.
questions.realTimeExample: An older framework kept the driver, the current ExtentTest and a 'currentUser' string as static fields. Under parallel runs, screenshots were attached to the wrong tests in the report. Converting those three fields to ThreadLocal values and creating page objects inside each test resolved the mix-ups.

questions.question: What is your strategy for maintaining a framework for parallel execution across both Selenium and Playwright?
questions.answer: The two tools isolate tests differently, so keep the principles common and the mechanics tool-specific. Selenium: one browser session per thread, held in ThreadLocal, with threads created by TestNG or JUnit and browsers supplied by a Grid. Playwright: its test runner starts several worker processes; each worker has its own browser, and each test gets a fresh, isolated BrowserContext (similar to a new incognito profile), so isolation is built in and cheaper than a new browser. In Playwright for Java, the objects are not thread-safe, so each thread creates its own Playwright instance. Shared strategy for both: (1) tests must be independent and runnable in any order; (2) each test creates its own unique data, preferably through APIs, and cleans it up; (3) no shared mutable state; (4) configuration such as base URL, credentials and worker or thread count comes from one place and can be overridden by the pipeline; (5) the worker count is tuned to the hardware; (6) flaky tests are tracked and fixed rather than hidden by retries; (7) CI splits the suite into shards across machines for both tools; (8) artifacts are kept per test: screenshots and logs for Selenium, traces and videos for Playwright.
questions.realTimeExample: A company runs a legacy Selenium suite and newer Playwright tests in the same pipeline. Both read the environment from the same configuration, create users through the same API helper with unique emails, and run as separate parallel jobs, so neither suite disturbs the other's data.

questions.question: How do you run cross-browser tests in parallel across Chrome, Edge and Firefox, including on cloud grids?
questions.answer: Parameterize the browser and let TestNG run the browsers at the same time. In testng.xml create one <test> block per browser, each passing a 'browser' parameter, and set parallel='tests' on the suite with a thread-count equal to the number of browsers. In the base class, read the value with @Parameters("browser") in @BeforeMethod, and have a driver factory create ChromeDriver, EdgeDriver or FirefoxDriver, stored in a ThreadLocal. The test classes are listed in each block, so the same tests run once per browser. To run on a Grid or a cloud provider, the factory creates a RemoteWebDriver with the matching Options object and the hub URL. Cloud grids such as BrowserStack, Sauce Labs and LambdaTest need your credentials and a vendor options block, set with setCapability, for the operating system, browser version and build name; keep the credentials in environment variables, not in code. Not every test must run on every browser: a common approach is the full suite on the main browser and a smaller critical set on the others.
questions.realTimeExample: The nightly pipeline runs 300 tests on Chrome and a 60-test critical set on Edge and Firefox in parallel through a cloud grid. A layout defect that appeared only in Firefox was caught by the critical set before release.
questions.javaCode:
<!-- testng.xml -->
<suite name="CrossBrowser" parallel="tests" thread-count="3">
    <test name="Chrome">
        <parameter name="browser" value="chrome"/>
        <classes><class name="tests.LoginTest"/></classes>
    </test>
    <test name="Edge">
        <parameter name="browser" value="edge"/>
        <classes><class name="tests.LoginTest"/></classes>
    </test>
    <test name="Firefox">
        <parameter name="browser" value="firefox"/>
        <classes><class name="tests.LoginTest"/></classes>
    </test>
</suite>

// BaseTest.java
@Parameters("browser")
@BeforeMethod
public void setUp(@Optional("chrome") String browser) throws MalformedURLException {
    String gridUrl = System.getProperty("gridUrl");      // null = run locally
    WebDriver driver;

    switch (browser.toLowerCase()) {
        case "edge":
            driver = gridUrl == null ? new EdgeDriver()
                    : new RemoteWebDriver(new URL(gridUrl), new EdgeOptions());
            break;
        case "firefox":
            driver = gridUrl == null ? new FirefoxDriver()
                    : new RemoteWebDriver(new URL(gridUrl), new FirefoxOptions());
            break;
        default:
            driver = gridUrl == null ? new ChromeDriver()
                    : new RemoteWebDriver(new URL(gridUrl), new ChromeOptions());
    }
    DriverManager.setDriver(driver);
}

questions.question: You have 100 test cases. How would you execute 20 in each browser?
questions.answer: 100 tests at 20 per browser means five browsers or browser configurations, for example Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari and headless Chrome. Split the tests into five sets of 20 and bind each set to one browser in testng.xml. There are two ways to form the sets. (1) By class or package: create five <test> blocks, each with its own 'browser' parameter and the classes or package that hold its 20 tests. (2) By group: tag tests with groups such as 'set1' to 'set5' and include one group in each <test> block. The base class reads the browser with @Parameters and creates the matching driver. Add parallel='tests' and thread-count='5' so the five sets run at the same time, each on its own browser. In the interview, also state the trade-off: this spreads tests across browsers to save time, so each test runs on only one browser. If the goal is full cross-browser coverage, every test should run on every browser, which is 500 executions.
questions.realTimeExample: A team has limited time on a cloud grid, so the 100 regression tests are divided by module: 20 login and profile tests on Chrome, 20 search tests on Firefox, 20 cart tests on Edge, 20 checkout tests on Safari and 20 order-history tests on headless Chrome, and the sets are rotated each night so every module is eventually run on every browser.
questions.javaCode:
<suite name="Distributed" parallel="tests" thread-count="5">
    <test name="Chrome - set 1">
        <parameter name="browser" value="chrome"/>
        <packages><package name="tests.login"/></packages>
    </test>
    <test name="Firefox - set 2">
        <parameter name="browser" value="firefox"/>
        <packages><package name="tests.search"/></packages>
    </test>
    <test name="Edge - set 3">
        <parameter name="browser" value="edge"/>
        <groups><run><include name="set3"/></run></groups>
        <packages><package name="tests.*"/></packages>
    </test>
    <!-- Safari - set 4 and Headless Chrome - set 5 follow the same pattern -->
</suite>

questions.question: How do you avoid test-data conflicts when thousands of tests run in parallel?
questions.answer: Conflicts happen when two tests read or change the same record at the same time. The principle is that each test owns its data. (1) Create fresh, unique data for every test, using a UUID or timestamp in names and emails, so no two tests can collide. (2) Create it quickly through APIs or direct database inserts in the test's setup, not through the UI. (3) When data cannot be created on demand, such as a limited set of pre-approved accounts, use a pool: a thread-safe queue from which a test takes an account, uses it exclusively and returns it at the end. (4) Treat shared reference data, such as product catalogues and country lists, as read-only; no test may modify it. (5) Tests that change global settings, like a feature flag or tax rate, affect everyone, so run them separately in a sequential group or in their own environment or tenant. (6) Never depend on data left behind by another test, and never assert on totals that other tests can change, such as 'the list has exactly 10 orders'; assert on your own record instead. (7) Keep per-thread state in ThreadLocal, not in static variables.
questions.realTimeExample: Two parallel tests used the same customer: one added an item to the cart while the other asserted the cart was empty, so one of them failed at random. Giving each test its own customer created through the API with a unique email removed the failures.

questions.question: What is your strategy for cleaning up test data created during parallel execution, including residual DB records after an unexpected crash?
questions.answer: Use two layers, because cleanup inside the test cannot be the only protection. Layer 1, each test cleans up after itself: record the ids of everything the test creates and delete them in @AfterMethod(alwaysRun = true), through an API or SQL, so it runs even when the test fails. Deleting by recorded id is safe in parallel because a test removes only its own records. Layer 2, a safety net for crashes: if the JVM, the agent or the pipeline is killed, the after-methods never run. So make all test data identifiable, with a prefix such as 'AUTO_' or a run id column or tag, and run a sweeper that deletes identifiable data older than a few hours. Run the sweeper at the start of each pipeline or as a scheduled job. The age condition is important: without it the sweeper could delete data that another run is still using. Other good options are to reset the environment completely, by restoring a database snapshot or starting a fresh database container for each run, and to design data with expiry where the system supports it. Whatever the method, never run automated deletion against production, and delete child records before parents to respect foreign keys.
questions.realTimeExample: A Jenkins agent was restarted mid-run, leaving 300 'AUTO_' customers and orders in the QA database, and later tests that counted search results began failing. A sweeper step was added at the start of the pipeline to delete AUTO_ records older than six hours, and the problem did not return.

questions.question: How would you cut suite execution time (for example 5,000 tests from 6 hours to under 1 hour, or 10 hours to 8)?
questions.answer: Measure first: get the duration of every test and find where the time goes, then act in order of gain. (1) Parallelize. This is the largest gain: going from 6 hours to 1 hour needs at least six parallel streams, realistically eight to ten to allow for overhead. Use TestNG threads with a ThreadLocal driver, a Grid sized for the load, and split the suite into shards across several CI machines. (2) Remove wasted time: replace every Thread.sleep and long implicit wait with explicit waits; this alone often gives the 20 percent needed to go from 10 hours to 8. (3) Shorten setup: create test data through APIs instead of UI steps, and log in once through the API, then inject the session cookie rather than using the login page in every test. (4) Move checks down the test pyramid: validations that do not need a browser, such as business rules and data combinations, run far faster as API tests. (5) Trim the suite: delete duplicate and low-value tests, and merge tests that repeat the same long flow. (6) Run by risk: a smoke set on every commit, the affected modules on pull requests and the full regression nightly. (7) Fix flaky tests, since retries cost time, and run headless on adequate hardware. Then report the before and after numbers.
questions.realTimeExample: A 5,000-test suite took 6 hours on a single thread. Running on 10 threads against a Docker Grid brought it to about 50 minutes; replacing fixed sleeps saved another 8 minutes, and logging in through the API with a cookie saved 5 more, giving a stable run of under 40 minutes.

questions.question: How do you identify, root-cause and fix flaky tests, in Selenium and in high-frequency CI pipelines?
questions.answer: A flaky test passes and fails on the same code without any change. Identify: use history, not impressions. Track the pass rate of each test across builds; a test that fails and then passes on rerun with no code change is flaky. Many CI and reporting tools show this. Reproduce it by running the test many times in a loop under CI-like conditions. Root cause: collect evidence for every failure (screenshot, page source, console and network logs, video, timestamps) and match it to the usual categories. (1) Timing: missing or wrong waits, animations, slow responses; the most common cause. (2) Test data: shared or leftover data. (3) Order dependency: passes alone, fails after a particular test. (4) Concurrency: shared static state under parallel runs. (5) Environment: slow agents, small window size, browser or driver version. (6) Unstable locators. (7) External dependencies such as third-party services. (8) A real intermittent defect in the product, such as a race condition, which must be reported, not patched in the test. Fix the cause: explicit waits on the right condition, isolated data, independent tests, ThreadLocal, stable test ids, mocks for third parties. In a high-frequency pipeline: quarantine a known flaky test with a ticket and an owner so it stops blocking merges but is not forgotten, allow at most one automatic retry and report retried tests, and review the flaky rate regularly with a target close to zero.
questions.realTimeExample: A nightly suite failed about 30 percent of the time. The history showed the same 12 tests failing in turn. Screenshots revealed a loading spinner still present at the failing click in eight of them, three shared one test user, and one depended on a third-party map widget. Adding waits for the spinner, giving unique users and mocking the map brought the pass rate to above 99 percent.

questions.question: How do you tell whether a failure is a genuine product defect or a flaky or script issue, and how do you classify them in triage?
questions.answer: Look at the evidence before rerunning anything. (1) Read the failure type. An assertion failure, where expected and actual values differ, suggests the application behaved differently and may be a defect. NoSuchElementException, a timeout or a stale element suggests a script, locator or timing problem, although a missing element can also mean the feature is broken. (2) Check the screenshot, page source, console errors and network responses at the moment of failure. A 500 response or a JavaScript error points to the product. (3) Reproduce manually with the same data and environment. If it fails by hand, it is a product defect. (4) Rerun the test alone several times. Consistent failure means a real problem in either product or script; intermittent failure means flakiness. (5) Check what changed: a new application build, a change to the test code or an environment change. (6) Check the scope: many unrelated tests failing together usually means the environment or the build, not individual defects. Classify each failure into one category with an owner: product defect (raise a bug with evidence, developers), automation or script issue (fix the script, QA), test data issue, environment or infrastructure issue (DevOps), or flaky and under investigation. Record the category in the report so trends are visible.
questions.realTimeExample: After a deployment, 40 tests failed. Triage found 35 failed at login with a 503 response, which was an environment issue as the auth service was down; 3 failed because a button's id was renamed, a script issue; and 2 showed a wrong order total that was reproduced manually, a genuine defect, which was logged with screenshots and the API response.

questions.question: A critical test fails in 1 out of every 100 executions. How do you find the root cause?
questions.answer: A 1 percent failure cannot be debugged by watching one run, so the method is to gather data and narrow down. (1) Capture everything on failure, automatically: screenshot, page source, console logs, network log, video, timestamps, the thread, the node and the test data used. (2) Reproduce in volume: run the test several hundred times in a loop, for example with invocationCount, in the same conditions where it fails: CI agent, headless, parallel. If it fails only in parallel, suspect shared state or data; if only on CI, suspect resources or timing. (3) Compare failing runs with passing runs and look for what is common to the failures: the same step, the same node, a slower response, a particular data value, a particular time. (4) Correlate with the application's server logs at the failure timestamp. (5) Form one hypothesis and test it by making the condition more likely: throttle the network or CPU, add an artificial delay to a response, or increase the load. If you can force the failure, you have found the cause. (6) Decide where the fault is. If the test acts before the application is ready, fix the wait. If the application itself misbehaves under a timing condition, that is a real race condition; a critical flow failing for 1 percent of users is a serious defect to report with the evidence, not something to hide with a retry.
questions.realTimeExample: A payment test failed about once in 100 runs with 'order not found'. Looping it 500 times with network logs showed that in every failure the confirmation page loaded before the order-creation call had returned. Adding a delay to that API made it fail every time. The cause was a product race condition, which the developers fixed by waiting for order creation before redirecting.

questions.question: How do you implement retry logic without hiding genuine failures or significantly increasing build time?
questions.answer: Retries are a safety net for infrastructure noise, not a way to make failing tests pass. The rules I apply: (1) Limit the count to one retry. A test that needs more than that is broken and should be fixed. (2) Make every retry visible. A test that passes on retry is reported as 'flaky' or 'passed on retry', counted, and reviewed; it is never shown as a clean pass. (3) Retry only failures that are likely to be environmental, such as a session not being created or a timeout, and do not retry assertion failures, because an assertion failure means the application returned a wrong result. (4) Set a threshold: if more than a small percentage of tests needed a retry, mark the build unstable, since widespread retries usually mean a real problem. (5) Keep the retry rate as a tracked metric and fix the top offenders every sprint. (6) To protect build time, retry only the failed tests, never the whole suite, keep waits efficient so a retry is short, and stop the run early when too many tests fail, since that indicates an environment outage. In TestNG, implement IRetryAnalyzer and attach it to all tests with an IAnnotationTransformer listener rather than editing each @Test.
questions.realTimeExample: A team had three retries on every test and a 'green' build that took 90 minutes and still let defects through, because a real intermittent defect passed on the third attempt. They reduced it to one retry for non-assertion failures and listed retried tests in the report. Build time fell to 55 minutes and two hidden product defects were found from the flaky list.

questions.question: Explain your automation framework in detail: architecture, components, folder structure, tools and core helper utilities.
questions.answer: Answer in a fixed order so it is easy to follow, and describe only what you have really used. (1) Type and tools: for example a hybrid framework using Java, Selenium WebDriver, TestNG, Maven, Page Object Model, Extent or Allure reports, Log4j2, Git and Jenkins. (2) Layers: a test layer with test classes holding only business steps and assertions; a page layer with one class per page holding locators and actions; a base layer with BaseTest for setup and teardown and a DriverFactory or DriverManager that creates the browser and keeps it in a ThreadLocal; a utility layer with wait helpers, config reader, Excel or JSON readers, screenshot and database or API helpers; and a listener layer for reporting, screenshots on failure and retry. (3) Configuration and data: properties files per environment and test data in JSON or Excel, both under src/test/resources. (4) Execution flow: Jenkins or the command line runs mvn test, Maven reads testng.xml, TestNG calls the listeners and @BeforeMethod, the driver starts, the test calls page methods, assertions run, the listener logs the result and captures a screenshot on failure, @AfterMethod quits the driver, and the report is generated and published. (5) Finish with your own contribution: what you built or improved.
questions.realTimeExample: "Our framework is a Java, Selenium and TestNG hybrid using the Page Object Model. I built the DriverFactory with ThreadLocal so we could run five threads on a Docker Grid, added the Extent listener that attaches screenshots to failed tests, and wrote the JSON data reader used by our DataProviders. The suite of 450 tests runs nightly from Jenkins in about 40 minutes."
