questions.question: How would you design a scalable automation framework from scratch (for example Java + TestNG, 5,000+ tests, no existing framework)? What does an ideal framework look like?
questions.answer: Start with requirements, not code: what application types (web, API, mobile), which browsers, how often it must run, who will write tests, and the CI tool. Then build in steps. (1) Foundation: Maven project, Selenium, TestNG, a clear package structure and coding standards. (2) Driver management: a DriverFactory supporting local, Grid and headless runs with a ThreadLocal driver, so parallel execution works from day one; adding it later is expensive. (3) Page Object Model with a BasePage of common wrapped actions that include explicit waits. (4) Configuration: environment and browser chosen at run time through properties and Maven profiles, with no hard-coded URLs or credentials. (5) Test data: external files and API-based data creation, unique per test. (6) Reporting, logging and screenshots through listeners. (7) An API layer for fast setup and for tests that do not need the UI. (8) CI integration with tagged suites: smoke, sanity, regression. (9) Governance: code reviews, a contribution guide and a flaky-test policy. For 5,000+ tests the deciding qualities are independence of tests, parallel and shardable execution, fast data setup and easy failure analysis. An ideal framework is maintainable (a UI change is fixed in one place), reusable, scalable, reliable (no flakiness), readable, fast, environment-independent, and gives clear reports. Prove the design with a small pilot of 20 to 30 tests before scaling.
questions.realTimeExample: On a new project with no automation, the first sprint delivered the skeleton, a driver factory, three page objects and five smoke tests running in Jenkins on every build. With that working end to end, the team added modules sprint by sprint, and the parallel-ready design let the suite grow to several thousand tests without restructuring.

questions.question: Have you built a framework from scratch? What automation challenges did you face while developing and maintaining it, and how did you overcome them?
questions.answer: Answer honestly about your role: built it alone, built it with a team, or enhanced an existing one, and name the parts you owned. Then give three or four real challenges in the form problem, action, result. Common ones: (1) Synchronization and flaky tests, solved by replacing sleeps with explicit-wait wrappers. (2) Dynamic elements and unstable locators, solved by stable attributes and by agreeing test ids with developers. (3) Parallel execution failures from a shared static driver, solved with ThreadLocal. (4) Test-data collisions, solved with unique data created through APIs. (5) Maintenance after frequent UI changes, solved by strict Page Object Model so each locator lives in one place. (6) Long execution time, solved with Grid, parallel runs and moving checks to API level. (7) Tests passing locally but failing in CI, solved with headless-specific window size and environment configuration. (8) Unclear reports, solved with screenshots, logs and step-level reporting. (9) Team adoption, solved with coding standards, reviews and documentation. Quote a measurable result where you can, such as run time or pass-rate improvement.
questions.realTimeExample: "I built the framework with one colleague; I owned the driver management and reporting. Our biggest problem was a 78 percent pass rate from timing issues. I wrote common click and type wrappers with explicit waits and removed about 200 Thread.sleep calls. The pass rate rose to 97 percent and the run became 25 minutes shorter."

questions.question: How do you design a hybrid automation framework?
questions.answer: A hybrid framework combines more than one framework approach so that each covers the other's weakness. The usual combination is: modular or Page Object Model for structure, where the application is split into page classes and reusable methods; data-driven, where test data lives in Excel, JSON or CSV and one test runs with many data sets through a TestNG DataProvider; and often keyword-driven or BDD, where test steps are written as keywords or Gherkin so less technical team members can read or write them. Design steps: create the page layer and base classes first; add the data layer with reader utilities and DataProviders; add configuration, reporting and logging; and add a keyword or Cucumber layer on top only if the team needs it, because it brings extra maintenance. The result is that test logic, test data and page details are all separate, so each can change without touching the others.
questions.realTimeExample: A login test is written once using LoginPage methods (modular). It runs for ten user types read from users.json through a DataProvider (data-driven). The product owner reads the scenarios because they are written in a Cucumber feature file (BDD). When the login button's locator changes, only LoginPage is edited.

questions.question: What is the purpose of using frameworks in testing, and what are their pros and cons?
questions.answer: An automation framework is an agreed structure, set of rules and reusable components for writing and running tests. Without one, every script repeats its own setup, locators, waits and data, and one change in the application breaks many scripts. Its purpose is to make automation maintainable and consistent across a team. Pros: reusability, since common code is written once; lower maintenance, since a change is fixed in one place; consistency, as everyone writes tests the same way; faster test creation after the initial setup; separation of test data and logic; built-in reporting, logging and screenshots; and easier CI/CD integration and scaling. Cons: a high initial cost in time and effort before the first useful test; skilled people are needed to design it; a learning curve for new team members; the framework itself must be maintained and upgraded; and a risk of over-engineering, where the framework becomes more complex than the tests need. For a very small or short-lived project the setup cost may not pay back.
questions.realTimeExample: A team had 150 standalone scripts, each with its own login code. When the login page changed, all 150 had to be edited. After moving to a framework with a single LoginPage class, the next login change took one edit and ten minutes.

questions.question: What is the Page Object Model? Why is it used, how have you implemented it, and what are its advantages, disadvantages and limitations?
questions.answer: The Page Object Model (POM) is a design pattern in which every page or major component of the application has its own class. The class holds that page's locators as private fields and the actions a user can perform there as public methods. Tests call these methods and never use locators directly. It is used to separate what is being tested (the test) from how the page is operated (the page class). Implementation: locators are private By fields; the driver is passed through the constructor; each method performs one user action; a method that navigates returns the next page's object; and assertions stay in the test class, not in the page class. Advantages: a UI change is fixed in one place; code is reused across tests; tests read like business steps; and less duplication. Disadvantages and limitations: more classes and more initial effort; large pages produce very large classes unless split into components; it does not by itself handle test data, waits or reporting; poorly designed page objects with assertions or test logic inside become hard to maintain; and for a very small project it can be more structure than needed.
questions.realTimeExample: The 'Login' button id changed from btnLogin to login-btn. Sixty tests use login, but only the one locator line in LoginPage was changed and all sixty tests passed again.

questions.question: How do you design page classes and the object repository for locator reusability, and how do you add new fields to it?
questions.answer: An object repository is the single place where locators are stored. In the Page Object Model, each page class is the repository for its own page. Design rules: (1) declare every locator once, as a private By field or a @FindBy element, with a meaningful name such as loginButton rather than btn1; (2) never write a locator inside a test; (3) put elements that appear on many pages, such as the header, footer, navigation menu and common pop-ups, in separate component classes that page classes reuse, instead of repeating them; (4) put shared behaviour, such as click, type and wait wrappers, in a BasePage that every page class extends; (5) for repeated elements that differ only by a value, write one method that builds the locator from a parameter instead of one locator per item. To add a new field: add one locator line to the relevant page class, add a public method that uses it, and call that method from the test. No other class changes, which is the benefit of the design.
questions.realTimeExample: A new 'Phone number' field was added to the registration form. The change was one new By field and one enterPhone() method in RegistrationPage, plus a call in the test. For the product list, a single method productLink(String name) serves every product instead of hundreds of separate locators.

questions.question: What is Page Factory? How is it different from POM, why is it used, and how does lazy element initialization work?
questions.answer: The Page Object Model is the design pattern: one class per page. Page Factory is a class provided by Selenium that is one way of implementing that pattern. Instead of By fields and findElement() calls, you declare WebElement fields with the @FindBy annotation and call PageFactory.initElements(driver, this) in the constructor. It is used because it makes page classes shorter and more readable. Lazy initialization: initElements() does not search for any element. It assigns each annotated field a proxy object. The real findElement() call happens only when a method is called on the field, and it happens again on every use. This means creating the page object never fails just because an element has not loaded yet, and the element is always looked up fresh. Adding @CacheLookup stores the element after the first lookup, which is faster for elements that never change but causes StaleElementReferenceException when the page re-renders. Related annotations are @FindBys (all conditions must match, like AND) and @FindAll (any condition, like OR). AjaxElementLocatorFactory can be passed to initElements to retry the lookup for a number of seconds. Limitations: @FindBy cannot build locators from run-time values and does not combine naturally with explicit waits on a By, so many teams today prefer plain By locators.
questions.realTimeExample: A page object for a dashboard is created immediately after login while the page is still loading. With Page Factory this does not throw an error, because nothing is searched until the test calls dashboard.openReports(), by which time the element exists.
buzzWords: POM Is the Pattern, Page Factory Is an Implementation

questions.question: If your application has 100 pages, do you create 100 page objects? How do you manage them efficiently?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. A page object represents a meaningful unit of the user interface, not a URL, so the number depends on the application. First, create classes only for the pages your tests actually use; there is no value in page objects for pages that are not automated. Second, reduce duplication: elements shared by many pages, such as the header, footer, side menu, search bar, pagination and date pickers, become component classes that are written once and reused by composition. Third, pages built from the same template, such as many similar list or form screens, can share one generic or parameterized page class. Fourth, a very large page is split into several smaller component classes, so sometimes one page has more than one class. To manage them: organize page classes in packages by module; let all of them extend a BasePage holding common actions; keep each class focused on a single responsibility; follow naming conventions; and optionally use a page manager or dependency injection to create page objects instead of writing 'new' everywhere. So the honest answer is that 100 pages might produce 60 or 130 classes, and that the count matters less than the absence of duplication.
questions.realTimeExample: An admin portal has 40 'master data' screens that all share the same layout: a search box, a grid and Add, Edit and Delete buttons. Instead of 40 page classes, one MasterDataPage class takes the screen name as a parameter, and a shared GridComponent handles the table on every screen.
buzzWords: Page Object per UI Unit, Not per URL

questions.question: How do you design the Page Object Model for single-page applications?
questions.answer: In a single-page application (SPA) built with React, Angular or Vue, the browser loads one page and JavaScript replaces parts of the screen, so there are no full page loads and often no clear 'pages'. Adjust the pattern in four ways. (1) Model components and views rather than pages: a class for each reusable component, such as the navigation bar, a modal, a data grid or a form, and a class for each view that composes those components. (2) Synchronize on elements, not on page load. The document reports 'complete' long before the data arrives, so every action waits for a specific element, for a loader to disappear or for the route in the URL to change. Give each view an 'is loaded' check that waits for a key element, and call it in the constructor or when navigating. (3) Avoid stale elements: SPAs re-render constantly, so store By locators and find the element at the moment of use; do not cache WebElements or use @CacheLookup. (4) Use stable locators: frameworks generate class names and ids, so rely on data-testid or accessibility attributes. Navigation methods still return the next view object so tests read as a flow.
questions.realTimeExample: In a React dashboard, clicking 'Orders' swaps the main panel without reloading. The OrdersView constructor waits for the orders grid to be visible and the spinner to disappear. Tests then use a shared GridComponent to filter and read rows, the same component used by the Customers and Invoices views.
buzzWords: Wait for Elements, Not Page Load

questions.question: How would you create a page object for the Amazon homepage?
questions.answer: Do not put the whole homepage in one class; it is large and most of it is shared with other pages. First identify the parts: a header (logo, delivery location, search box with category dropdown, account menu, cart icon), a navigation bar, the main content with banners and product cards, and a footer. The header and footer appear on every Amazon page, so they become component classes reused everywhere. The HomePage class then contains only what is unique to the home page and exposes the components. Include only elements your tests need, name methods after user actions (searchFor, openCart, getCartCount), keep locators private, add explicit waits, and make methods that navigate return the next page object, for example searchFor() returns SearchResultsPage. Assertions stay in the tests. The ids used below are the ones Amazon has used for a long time, but always confirm them in DevTools because live sites change.
questions.realTimeExample: A test opens the home page, searches for 'wireless mouse' through the header component, and asserts on the results page that results are shown. A second test reuses the same HeaderComponent from the product page to open the cart, with no duplicated locators.

questions.question: How do you manage locators through centralized JSON files?
questions.answer: In this approach locators are kept outside the Java code, in JSON files, usually one file per page. Each entry has a logical name, a locator type (id, css, xpath) and a value. A small utility loads the file once, caches it, and converts an entry into a Selenium By object when a page method asks for it by name. Benefits: locators can be updated without recompiling; the same page class can serve variants, such as different locators for web and mobile or for different brands or languages, by loading a different file; and all locators are visible in one place. Costs, which you should also state: you lose compile-time checking and IDE navigation, so a misspelt key fails only at run time; there is one more layer to maintain; and the file can drift from the code. To keep it safe, validate the files at start-up, fail with a clear message naming the missing key, use constants for key names, and keep the files in version control with the code. For most single-application projects, By fields inside page classes are simpler; JSON repositories are worth it when locators genuinely vary by platform or brand.
questions.realTimeExample: One codebase tests three branded versions of the same shopping site whose pages behave the same but have different ids. A 'brand' property selects which locator folder to load, so the page classes and tests are shared across all three brands.
buzzWords: Convert to By at Run Time

questions.question: How do you manage test data in your framework and pass it to scripts?
questions.answer: The first rule is that test data is never hard-coded in test methods. Keep different kinds of data in the place that suits them. (1) Configuration data such as URLs, browser and timeouts: properties files per environment. (2) Static test data such as input combinations and expected messages: JSON, Excel or CSV files under src/test/resources, read by utility classes. (3) Dynamic data that must be unique, such as a new user's email: generated at run time with a UUID, timestamp or a library such as Java Faker. (4) Pre-condition data such as an existing customer with an order: created through APIs or database scripts in setup and removed in teardown. (5) Secrets such as passwords and API keys: environment variables or the CI tool's secret store, never committed to Git. Ways to pass data to scripts: TestNG @DataProvider for running one test with many data sets; @Parameters with testng.xml for values like browser; system properties from the Maven command line (-Denv=qa); POJO classes that map JSON into typed objects; and Examples tables in Cucumber. Also keep data separate per environment and make each test own its data so tests can run in parallel.
questions.realTimeExample: A registration test reads valid and invalid field combinations from registration.json through a DataProvider, generates a unique email for each run, reads the base URL from qa.properties, and takes the admin password from a Jenkins credential exposed as an environment variable.

questions.question: How do you implement data-driven testing with Excel, CSV or JSON, and how would you design the utility that reads Excel, CSV or DB data (for example first row, first cell)?
questions.answer: Data-driven testing means one test method runs many times with different data sets kept outside the code. In TestNG the link between the file and the test is a @DataProvider that returns Object[][] (or an Iterator), where each row is one test run. Readers: Excel is read with Apache POI (XSSFWorkbook for .xlsx): workbook, then sheet, then row, then cell, all indexed from 0, so the first row and first cell is getRow(0).getCell(0). Use DataFormatter to read every cell as text, otherwise numeric and date cells throw errors when read as strings. CSV can be read with OpenCSV or a simple line split, and JSON with Jackson or Gson, mapped to POJOs. Database data is read with JDBC. Utility design: one small class per source with a single clear responsibility; methods that take the file and sheet name and return a neutral structure such as List<Map<String, String>> keyed by column header, so tests do not depend on column positions; resources closed with try-with-resources; missing files or sheets reported with a clear message; and no static mutable state so it is safe in parallel. JSON is the easiest format for version control and code review; Excel suits teams where non-programmers maintain the data.
questions.realTimeExample: Login data for 25 user types is kept in LoginData.xlsx with the columns username, password and expected. The DataProvider calls ExcelReader.read(), which skips the header row, and the single login test runs 25 times, each reported as its own result.

questions.question: How do you manage environment configuration (QA, UAT, Staging, Prod): central config files, Maven profiles and build tools?
questions.answer: The goal is that the same test code runs on any environment and only configuration changes. (1) Keep one properties file per environment (qa.properties, uat.properties, staging.properties, prod.properties) under src/test/resources/config, each holding the base URL, API URL, database details and timeouts. (2) Select the environment at run time with a system property: mvn test -Denv=uat. A ConfigReader reads the 'env' property, defaults to QA, loads the matching file once and serves values to the whole framework. (3) Allow overrides: a value given on the command line or as an environment variable takes priority over the file, which lets the pipeline change a single value. (4) Maven profiles are an alternative or an addition: each <profile> sets properties such as env and the suite file, and is activated with -Pqa or -Puat. (5) Keep secrets out of the files; read them from environment variables or the CI secret store. (6) In Jenkins, expose environment and browser as build parameters and pass them into the Maven command. (7) Guard production: allow only read-only smoke tests there and block tests tagged as data-changing. Libraries such as Owner can replace a hand-written ConfigReader.
questions.realTimeExample: The same regression suite runs nightly on QA with 'mvn test -Pqa' and before each release on Staging with 'mvn test -Pstaging'. Nothing in the test or page classes changes; the profile decides which properties file the ConfigReader loads.

questions.question: How do you keep test data isolated and configured per environment (QA versus Staging versus Prod)?
questions.answer: Each environment has its own database, so data that exists in QA may not exist in Staging. Handle this in four ways. (1) Environment-specific data files: keep data in folders per environment, such as testdata/qa and testdata/staging, with the same file names and structure, and let the framework load the folder matching the selected environment. Tests refer to logical names such as 'premiumCustomer', never to a raw id. (2) Prefer creating data at run time through APIs, because created data works in every environment and needs no per-environment files. (3) Separate accounts and credentials per environment, stored in the secret store under environment-specific names, so a QA test can never log in to Production by mistake. (4) Rules per environment: QA allows full create, update and delete with cleanup; Staging or UAT is closer to production data, so use dedicated test accounts and avoid touching data that business users are checking; Production allows only read-only smoke checks with a dedicated test account and never destructive tests. Enforce this technically with groups or tags, for example excluding a 'destructive' group when env is prod, and with a guard in the base class. Where production-like data is copied to lower environments, it must be masked so that no real personal data is exposed.
questions.realTimeExample: The test 'premium customer sees free shipping' uses the key premiumCustomer. In QA that resolves to customer 1042 and in Staging to customer 88213, each from its own data file. In Production the test is skipped because it places an order and is tagged 'destructive'.

questions.question: What is your strategy for writing reusable utilities and keeping scripts maintainable as the project grows?
questions.answer: Reusability: follow the DRY principle (Don't Repeat Yourself). When the same code appears a second or third time, move it into a shared place. Typical utilities are element-action wrappers (click, type, select with built-in waits), wait helpers, config and data readers, screenshot and report helpers, date and random-data generators, and API and database helpers. Design rules: each utility does one job (single responsibility); methods are small, take parameters instead of hard-coded values and have clear names; utilities are stateless so they are safe in parallel; and errors give a clear message. Avoid one giant 'CommonUtils' class with hundreds of unrelated methods. Maintainability: strict Page Object Model so locators exist once; tests contain only business steps and assertions; no hard-coded data, URLs or sleeps; consistent naming and package structure; independent tests; code reviews and static analysis for every change; version control with small pull requests; regular refactoring and removal of dead or duplicate tests; documentation in a README; and dependencies kept up to date. A useful measure is how many files must change when one screen changes; the answer should be one.
questions.realTimeExample: Five different test classes each had their own code to pick a date from the calendar. It was moved into one DatePickerComponent.selectDate() method. When the calendar widget was later replaced, one method was rewritten instead of five.

questions.question: How would you design reusable, thread-safe utilities for parallel execution?
questions.answer: A utility is thread-safe when many test threads can use it at the same time without affecting each other. Rules: (1) Make utilities stateless: a method receives everything it needs as parameters, including the driver, and keeps nothing in fields, so there is nothing to share. (2) Never keep mutable state in static fields. A static WebDriver, WebDriverWait, 'current test' or 'last response' variable is shared by all threads and is the usual cause of parallel failures. (3) Where per-thread state is required, such as the driver or the current report entry, store it in a ThreadLocal and remove it in teardown. (4) Shared read-only data, such as loaded configuration, is safe: load it once and never modify it, and make such fields final. (5) Where threads must share and modify a structure, use the concurrent collections, ConcurrentHashMap or CopyOnWriteArrayList, or AtomicInteger for counters, rather than HashMap, ArrayList and int. (6) Initialize shared objects once in a thread-safe way, using a static initializer or computeIfAbsent. (7) Be careful with classes that are not thread-safe: SimpleDateFormat should be replaced with DateTimeFormatter, and a workbook or file should not be written by several threads; give each thread its own output file or synchronize the write. (8) Use unique names for files, such as screenshots, including the thread id or a UUID.
questions.realTimeExample: A screenshot utility named files only by test name, and a shared 'static int counter' numbered them. In parallel runs, screenshots overwrote each other and the counter skipped values. Adding the thread id and a timestamp to the name, and replacing the counter with an AtomicInteger, fixed both issues.

questions.question: Which reporting tool do you use and why? How do you generate Extent, Allure or HTML reports, customise them after execution and embed error logs? Write custom-report code.
questions.answer: TestNG produces basic HTML reports by default (emailable-report.html and index.html in test-output), but they are plain. Most frameworks add Extent Reports or Allure. Extent Reports is a library you drive from code: create an ExtentReports object, attach an ExtentSparkReporter with the output file, create an ExtentTest for each test, log steps and results, and call flush() at the end to write the file. It produces a single self-contained HTML file that is easy to email, with a dashboard, pass and fail charts, categories and embedded screenshots. Allure collects result files during the run through the allure-testng dependency and then builds a rich interactive report with 'allure serve' or the Jenkins Allure plugin; it supports @Step, @Attachment, history and trends. Choose Extent for a simple shareable file and Allure for trends and CI integration. Wire reporting through a TestNG ITestListener so tests contain no reporting code. Customization: set the report name, title and theme; add system information such as environment, browser and build number; assign categories and authors; and embed the exception, console logs and a screenshot on failure. 'After execution' customization means the code in onFinish that adds summary information before flush(), or post-processing in the pipeline such as publishing the report and emailing the summary. For parallel runs, keep the ExtentTest in a ThreadLocal.
questions.realTimeExample: After the nightly run, Jenkins publishes the Extent report showing 438 passed, 9 failed and 3 skipped on QA with Chrome 131. Each failed test opens to show the steps, the exception and the screenshot at the point of failure, so triage starts without rerunning anything.

questions.question: How do you capture screenshots only for failed tests using TestNG listeners and attach them to the Extent or HTML report?
questions.answer: Use the TestNG ITestListener interface. Its onTestFailure(ITestResult result) method is called automatically, and only, when a test fails, so placing the screenshot code there captures failures alone and keeps test classes free of screenshot code. Steps: (1) create a class that implements ITestListener; (2) in onTestFailure, get the driver for the current thread, usually from a ThreadLocal DriverManager; (3) take the screenshot with TakesScreenshot, either as BASE64 to embed directly in the report, which keeps the report a single portable file, or as a FILE saved with a unique name and linked by path; (4) attach it to the report entry for that test, along with the exception from result.getThrowable(); (5) register the listener in testng.xml with the <listeners> tag, or with @Listeners on the base class. One timing point: the listener's onTestFailure runs before @AfterMethod, so the browser is still open when the screenshot is taken. An alternative without a listener is an @AfterMethod that checks result.getStatus() == ITestResult.FAILURE.
questions.realTimeExample: A checkout test fails overnight in Jenkins. The Extent report shows the failed test with the assertion message and a screenshot showing an 'Out of stock' pop-up covering the Pay button, so the cause is clear without rerunning the test.

questions.question: What is Log4j/Log4j2, and why do we use logging in a Selenium framework?
questions.answer: Log4j2 is an open-source logging library for Java from Apache; it is the current version, and the original Log4j 1.x is retired. It records messages from the code as it runs, with a timestamp, a level, the class name and the text, and sends them to one or more destinations such as the console or a file, controlled by a configuration file (log4j2.xml) rather than by code. In a Selenium framework logging is used because a report shows that a test failed, while the log shows what happened before the failure. Benefits: (1) debugging failures in CI or overnight runs that nobody watched; (2) a step-by-step trail of actions, such as 'Opening URL', 'Clicked Login', 'Order id captured'; (3) faster triage, since the log shows whether the fault was the test data, the environment or the application; (4) control without code changes, since the level can be raised or lowered in the configuration; (5) better than System.out.println, which has no levels, timestamps or files and cannot be switched off. Good practice is to log inside the common wrapper methods and listeners so that every action is recorded once, and never to log passwords or other secrets.
questions.realTimeExample: A test failed at 2 a.m. with 'element not found'. The log showed 'ERROR Login API returned 503' three lines earlier, which made it clear the environment was down and the script was not at fault.

questions.question: What are the log levels in Log4j2?
questions.answer: A log level states how important a message is. Log4j2 has six standard levels, from least to most severe: TRACE, the finest detail, such as every small step; DEBUG, information useful when diagnosing a problem, such as locator values and data used; INFO, normal progress messages, such as 'Test started' or 'User logged in'; WARN, something unexpected that did not stop the test, such as a retry or a slow response; ERROR, a failure of an operation, such as an element not found or an assertion failure; and FATAL, a severe failure that stops the run, such as the browser failing to start. There are also two special settings: ALL turns on everything and OFF turns logging off. The level set in the configuration is a threshold: that level and everything more severe is written, and anything less severe is ignored. With the level at INFO you get INFO, WARN, ERROR and FATAL but not DEBUG or TRACE. Typical use is INFO for regular CI runs and DEBUG when investigating a failure.
questions.realTimeExample: Nightly runs use INFO so the logs stay small. When a test started failing only on Jenkins, the level was changed to DEBUG in log4j2.xml for one run, which revealed the exact locator and wait values used, and was then set back to INFO.
buzzWords: TRACE < DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR < FATAL

questions.question: What is the use of appenders in Log4j2?
questions.answer: Log4j2 has three main parts. A Logger captures the message in the code. An Appender decides where the message is sent. A Layout decides how the message is formatted. So an appender is the destination of the log output. Common appenders: ConsoleAppender writes to the console, which is useful while developing and appears in the Jenkins console output; FileAppender writes to a single file; RollingFileAppender writes to a file and starts a new one when a size or time limit is reached, keeping a set number of old files, which stops log files growing without limit; and there are others such as JDBC (database), SMTP (email) and Async appenders for performance. Several appenders can be attached to one logger, so the same message can go to the console and to a file. Each appender has a layout, usually PatternLayout, defining the format, for example date, level, class and message. Appenders are declared in log4j2.xml and linked to loggers with AppenderRef, so destinations can be changed without touching code.
questions.realTimeExample: The framework sends INFO messages to the console for a quick view in Jenkins and writes everything from DEBUG upward to logs/automation.log through a rolling file appender that starts a new file every 10 MB and keeps the last five, which is attached to the build as an artifact.
questions.javaCode:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<Configuration status="WARN">
    <Appenders>
        <Console name="Console" target="SYSTEM_OUT">
            <PatternLayout pattern="%d{HH:mm:ss} %-5level %c{1} - %msg%n"/>
        </Console>

        <RollingFile name="File" fileName="logs/automation.log"
                     filePattern="logs/automation-%d{yyyy-MM-dd}-%i.log">
            <PatternLayout pattern="%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} [%t] %-5level %c{1} - %msg%n"/>
            <Policies>
                <SizeBasedTriggeringPolicy size="10 MB"/>
            </Policies>
            <DefaultRolloverStrategy max="5"/>
        </RollingFile>
    </Appenders>

    <Loggers>
        <Root level="debug">
            <AppenderRef ref="Console" level="info"/>
            <AppenderRef ref="File"/>
        </Root>
    </Loggers>
</Configuration>

questions.question: How do you integrate Selenium with other tools (TestNG/JUnit, Maven/Gradle, Jenkins, Allure/Extent, Git)?
questions.answer: Selenium only drives the browser, so a working framework connects it to a tool for each other job. Build tool, Maven or Gradle: declares Selenium, TestNG and reporting libraries as dependencies in pom.xml, downloads them, compiles the code and runs the tests with one command (mvn test) through the Surefire plugin. Test framework, TestNG or JUnit: provides @Test, setup and teardown annotations, assertions, grouping, data providers and parallel execution; testng.xml defines what runs and Surefire points to it. Reporting, Extent or Allure: added as a dependency and fed through a TestNG listener, so results, steps and screenshots become an HTML report. Version control, Git: the framework lives in a repository on GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket; engineers work on branches and merge through pull requests. CI/CD, Jenkins: a job or Jenkinsfile checks out the code from Git, runs the Maven command with parameters such as environment and browser, on a schedule or after each build, then publishes the report and sends notifications. Around these sit Log4j2 for logging, Selenium Grid or Docker for browsers, and Apache POI or Jackson for test data. The chain is: Git supplies the code, Jenkins triggers Maven, Maven runs TestNG, TestNG runs the Selenium tests, and the listener produces the report.
questions.realTimeExample: A developer merges a change at 4 p.m. Jenkins detects the new build, checks out the automation repository, runs 'mvn clean test -Psmoke -Denv=qa' against the Docker Grid, publishes the Allure report and posts '62 passed, 1 failed' with the link in the team channel within 15 minutes.

<dependencies>

    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.testng</groupId>
        <artifactId>testng</artifactId>
        <version>7.10.2</version>
        <scope>test</scope>

</dependencies>

<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>

</build>

questions.question: How do you execute your automation suite, and what changes or pre-requisites do you set up before a run?
questions.answer: Ways to execute: from the IDE by running a test class or testng.xml while developing; from the command line with Maven, for example mvn clean test -Denv=qa -Dbrowser=chrome -Dgroups=smoke, which is what the pipeline also uses; and from CI, where a Jenkins job runs on a schedule, on each new build or on demand with parameters. Pre-requisites before a run: (1) the right code, by pulling the latest from the main branch; (2) the environment, by confirming the application URL is up and the correct build is deployed, often with a quick health check or smoke test; (3) configuration, by selecting the environment, browser, headless mode, thread count and the suite or groups to run; (4) test data, by making sure required accounts and data exist or are created by setup scripts, and that old test data is cleaned; (5) infrastructure, by checking that the Grid or cloud nodes are available and that browser and driver versions are compatible; (6) access, such as VPN, credentials and any CAPTCHA or OTP bypass in the test environment; (7) clean output folders for reports and screenshots. After the run, review the report, triage the failures and share the summary.
questions.realTimeExample: Before the nightly regression, the pipeline's first stage calls the application's health endpoint and runs five smoke tests. If either fails, the full run is skipped and the team is notified that the environment is down, instead of producing 400 false failures.

questions.question: How often do you trigger regression scripts, and how do you manage them in the repository?
questions.answer: Frequency depends on the size of the suite, so run different layers at different times. Smoke tests, a few minutes long, run on every build or deployment to the test environment. A sanity or module-level set runs on pull requests or when a module changes. The full regression runs nightly on the latest build, so results are ready each morning, and again before every release on the release candidate. Longer cross-browser runs are often weekly. Tests are also triggered on demand, for example after a hotfix. Managing them in the repository: the framework and all tests are in Git; the main branch always holds stable, passing tests; new or changed tests are written on feature branches and merged through pull requests after review and a passing run; tests are tagged with TestNG groups such as smoke, sanity and regression, and by module, so any subset can be selected without changing code; suite XML files define the standard runs; flaky or blocked tests are marked or quarantined with a linked ticket rather than deleted or left failing; and where releases are maintained in parallel, the test branch or tag matches the application version.
questions.realTimeExample: A team runs 40 smoke tests on each deployment (6 minutes), the 900-test regression every night at 1 a.m. (45 minutes on the Grid), and the same regression on the release branch before sign-off. A test for a feature still in development sits on a feature branch until the feature is merged.

questions.question: Do you follow sprint (in-sprint) automation or regression automation?
questions.answer: They are two approaches and most mature teams use both. In-sprint automation means the tests for a user story are automated in the same sprint in which the story is developed, and automation is part of the Definition of Done. Its advantages are fast feedback and no backlog of un-automated tests; its difficulty is that the UI is still changing during the sprint. It works when QA is involved from story refinement, locators or test ids are agreed with developers early, API-level tests are written first because APIs stabilise sooner than the UI, and page objects are prepared from designs. Regression automation, sometimes called N-1 automation, means stable features from previous sprints are automated afterwards and added to the regression suite. It is easier because the feature no longer changes, but automation always lags behind and manual regression effort stays high. A practical answer: 'We aim for in-sprint automation of new stories, starting with API tests and adding the main UI flows once the screens are stable. Anything not finished is carried as automation debt into the next sprint, and each in-sprint test joins the regression pack that runs nightly.' Say truthfully which one your team does.
questions.realTimeExample: For a 'save for later' story, API tests for the new endpoint were written on day three of the sprint, the page object was built from the design on day five, and two UI tests were completed on day eight once the screen was stable. All were merged before the sprint ended and now run in the nightly regression.

questions.question: What factors do you consider when selecting an automation tool for a project?
questions.answer: Match the tool to the project instead of choosing by popularity. Factors: (1) Application type and technology: web, mobile, desktop or API, and special elements such as iframes, shadow DOM or canvas. (2) Browser and platform coverage required, including Safari and real mobile devices. (3) Team skills: the programming languages the team knows and whether non-programmers must write tests. (4) Cost: licence fees versus open source, plus the cost of infrastructure, training and maintenance. (5) Integration with the existing ecosystem: CI/CD tool, test management, defect tracker and reporting. (6) Capabilities: parallel execution, automatic waiting, network mocking, debugging aids such as traces and video, and API testing support. (7) Community, documentation, vendor support and how actively the tool is maintained. (8) Stability and speed of execution, and the maintenance effort when the application changes. (9) Scalability for the expected size of the suite. (10) Organisational constraints such as security policies and approved tools. The final step is a proof of concept: automate a few representative, difficult scenarios with the two shortlisted tools and compare the results before deciding.
questions.realTimeExample: For a new React web application with a team strong in TypeScript and no legacy tests, a proof of concept compared Selenium and Playwright on five scenarios including a file download and an API mock. Playwright was chosen for its auto-waiting and built-in tracing. For another project with a large Java team and an existing Selenium Grid, Selenium was kept.

questions.question: Given TOSCA, LoadRunner and Selenium, which tool would you use for which kind of testing?
questions.answer: Each tool is built for a different purpose. Selenium is an open-source, code-based tool for functional and regression testing of web applications across browsers. Use it when the application is web-based, the team can program, and cost and flexibility matter. It does not test performance, desktop applications or packaged enterprise software. Tosca (Tricentis) is a licensed, model-based, scriptless tool for end-to-end functional and regression automation. Use it for enterprise packaged applications such as SAP, Salesforce and Oracle, and for business processes that cross web, desktop, API and mainframe systems, especially when testers are business analysts rather than programmers. Its drawbacks are licence cost and vendor dependence. LoadRunner (OpenText, formerly Micro Focus) is a performance testing tool. Use it for load, stress, endurance and spike testing: it simulates thousands of virtual users at protocol level and measures response time, throughput and server resource usage. It is not for functional testing. So: Selenium for web functional and regression tests, Tosca for scriptless end-to-end and packaged-application automation, and LoadRunner for performance. They complement each other and can be used on the same project.
questions.realTimeExample: A bank automates its customer web portal regression with Selenium, its SAP-based back-office processes with Tosca, and before each major release uses LoadRunner to confirm the portal handles 5,000 concurrent users with response times under three seconds.

questions.question: I give you a website to automate. How do you proceed, and what questions do you ask first?
questions.answer: Begin with questions, because the answers decide the design. About the goal: what is the purpose of automation (regression, smoke, cross-browser), and what does success look like? About scope: which modules and flows are business-critical, are there existing manual test cases, and what should not be automated? About the application: which technology is it built with, how stable is the UI, are there iframes, CAPTCHA, OTP, file uploads or third-party integrations, and can developers add test ids? About environments and data: which environments exist, how is test data created, and are APIs available for setup? About execution: which browsers and devices, how often will it run, and which CI tool is used? About the team: skills, timeline and who will maintain the tests. Then proceed in steps: explore the application manually to understand the flows; choose candidates by risk and repetition; pick the tool and stack and confirm with a short proof of concept; set up the framework skeleton with driver management, page objects, configuration and reporting; automate the smoke flows first and get them running in CI; expand module by module with code reviews; and review results and maintain regularly.
questions.realTimeExample: Asked to automate an insurance quote website, the engineer first learned that only Chrome and Edge mattered, that quotes needed a CAPTCHA that could be disabled in QA, and that ten flows covered 80 percent of usage. Those ten flows were automated first and ran in Jenkins within two weeks.

questions.question: How do you automate a feature that is not yet fully developed?
questions.answer: Start on everything that does not depend on the finished UI, and prepare the rest so it can be completed quickly. (1) Understand the feature from the user story, acceptance criteria and UI designs, and write the test scenarios and test data now. (2) Agree locators with the developers in advance, ideally data-testid attributes, so page objects can be written before the screen exists. (3) Build the page object classes and test methods as a skeleton, using the agreed locators and marking unfinished parts clearly. (4) Automate at API level first: if the API contract (for example a Swagger or OpenAPI document) is available, write API tests, and use mocks or stubs such as WireMock for endpoints that are not ready. (5) Prepare reusable parts: test data creation, utilities and navigation up to the new feature. (6) Keep unfinished tests out of the main regression run, for example with enabled = false or a 'wip' group, so they do not create false failures. (7) When the feature is deployed, verify the locators, run and stabilise the tests, and move them into the regression pack. This is shift-left testing: working in parallel with development rather than waiting for it to finish.
questions.realTimeExample: For a 'wishlist' feature still in development, the QA engineer wrote API tests against the agreed contract using a WireMock stub, created WishlistPage with the test ids from the design review, and kept the UI tests in a 'wip' group. When the feature reached QA, only two locators needed adjusting and the tests were enabled the same day.

questions.question: You have been asked to automate a legacy application or convert a legacy manual regression suite. What is your approach?
questions.answer: Do not try to automate everything one-for-one. (1) Assess: learn the application's technology, since legacy systems often have old browsers, frames, pop-up windows, missing ids and little documentation, and confirm feasibility with a proof of concept on a few difficult screens. (2) Review the manual suite before automating: remove obsolete and duplicate cases, merge overlapping ones, and fill gaps. Old suites usually shrink considerably at this step. (3) Prioritize by value: rank the remaining cases by business criticality, how often they are executed, stability of the feature, and effort to automate. Automate high-value, stable, repetitive cases first; leave rare, unstable or highly visual cases manual. (4) Build or extend the framework to suit the legacy quirks, for example robust locator strategies based on labels and relative XPath, frame and window helpers, and where possible ask for test ids to be added. (5) Convert in phases: smoke flows first, then critical regression module by module, and move checks to the API or database level where an interface exists, because that is faster and more stable than the UI. (6) Run automated tests alongside the manual ones for a few cycles to build trust, then retire the manual cases. (7) Track and report progress: cases automated, manual hours saved and defects found. (8) Document as you go, because the automation becomes the living description of how the legacy system behaves.
questions.realTimeExample: A 1,200-case manual regression for a ten-year-old claims system was reviewed down to 700 valid cases. The 250 most critical and most repeated were automated in the first three months, cutting the manual regression cycle from eight days to three, and the rest followed in priority order.

questions.question: Manual test cases need urgent automation within 2 days. What is your strategy?
questions.answer: With a fixed deadline the scope must be controlled, so prioritize and be open about what will and will not be done. (1) Clarify the purpose: why two days, and which release or demo depends on it. That tells you what must be covered. (2) Prioritize strictly: select the business-critical, high-risk, happy-path flows that can realistically be completed, and agree the list with the lead or product owner in writing. (3) Reuse what exists: current page objects, utilities, login and data setup. Do not build new framework features under deadline. (4) Take the fastest reliable route: create pre-condition data through APIs, automate checks at API level where the UI adds no value, and use data-driven tests to cover variations with one script. (5) Divide the work among the team by module so people do not block each other, with short check-ins. (6) Keep the minimum quality bar: explicit waits, meaningful assertions and a peer review, even if brief. A fast but flaky test is of no use. (7) Run the tests several times and in the pipeline before handing over. (8) Communicate: report what is automated, what remains manual and the plan for the rest, and note any shortcuts as technical debt to fix afterwards.
questions.realTimeExample: Given 60 manual cases and two days before a release, the team agreed to automate the 18 cases covering login, search, checkout and payment. Two engineers split them by module, reused existing page objects, and delivered 18 stable tests in CI. The remaining 42 were run manually for that release and automated over the next sprint.

questions.question: A script worked yesterday but fails today, or the suite started failing after a deployment. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.answer: Something changed, so the task is to find what. (1) Read the evidence first: the error message and stack trace, the screenshot, the logs and the report. Identify the exact step and the type of failure. (2) Look at the pattern: one test or many? If most tests fail at the same early step, such as login, suspect the environment or the build, not the individual scripts. (3) Check the environment: is the application up, is the correct build deployed, are dependent services and the database available, has test data been reset or expired? (4) Check what changed in the application: read the release notes or commit list for the deployment and reproduce the failing step manually. If it fails manually too, it is a product defect or an intended change. (5) Check what changed on the automation side: recent commits to the test code, an updated dependency, or a browser or driver auto-update. (6) Rerun the failing test alone to see whether the failure is consistent or intermittent. (7) Classify and act: for a product defect, raise a bug with evidence; for an intended application change, update the page object or expected value; for an environment or data problem, fix it or report it to the owner and rerun; for a flaky script, fix the wait or the data. (8) Share a short summary of the cause and consider a prevention step, such as a smoke check after deployment or developers flagging UI changes in advance.
questions.realTimeExample: After a Tuesday deployment, 120 of 400 tests failed. All 120 failed at the address form. The release notes showed that 'Postcode' had been split into two fields. This was an intended change, so AddressPage was updated in one place and the suite returned to green; the team then asked for UI changes to be mentioned in the deployment notes.

questions.question: The application has minor changes that break scripts. How do you approach modifying the automation?
questions.answer: A well-structured framework makes a minor change a small edit. (1) Understand the change: confirm from the story, release notes or the developer that it is intended and not a defect, and learn exactly what changed, whether a locator, a label, an extra field or a different flow. (2) Find the impact: identify which page objects and tests use the changed element; because locators live only in page classes, this is usually one class. (3) Make the change in the right layer. A changed locator is one line in the page class. A new field is one locator and one method, plus the call in affected tests. Changed text is an update to the expected value in the test data. A changed flow means updating the page methods and the tests that use them. Do not patch individual test scripts with local workarounds. (4) Run the affected tests, then the related regression, to confirm nothing else broke. (5) Commit on a branch with a clear message referring to the story, and merge after review. (6) Reduce future breakage: use stable locators such as test ids, and ask to be told about UI changes during the sprint so automation is updated together with the feature rather than after failures.
questions.realTimeExample: The 'Sign in' button text changed to 'Log in' and its id from signin to login-btn. The fix was a single locator line in LoginPage and one expected value in the test data file, after which the 40 tests that use login passed again.

questions.question: A test fails (say at line 98 of 100). What is your next step?
questions.answer: Do not simply rerun it and move on; find out why it failed. (1) Read the exception and the stack trace. The exception type shows the kind of problem, the message gives the detail and the stack trace gives the exact line. (2) Look at the screenshot and logs captured at the failure to see the state of the application at that moment. (3) Look at the lines before the failure too. A failure at line 98 is often caused by something earlier, such as a step that did not really succeed or data that was not saved; the failing line is only where the problem became visible. (4) Reproduce it: run the test alone, in debug mode with a breakpoint just before the failing line, and inspect the variables and the page. Also perform the steps manually. (5) Decide the category. If the application behaves wrongly, it is a defect: log it with steps, data, screenshot and logs. If the locator, wait, data or logic in the script is wrong, fix the script. If the environment or test data is the cause, fix or report that. If it passes on rerun without any change, treat it as flaky and investigate rather than ignore it. (6) After a fix, rerun the test several times and then the related tests. Remember that when a test stops at line 98, lines 99 and 100 were never checked, so those verifications are still unknown.
questions.realTimeExample: A test failed at the final assertion, 'order total expected 1180, found 1000'. The screenshot showed the total without tax. Debugging showed the 'apply tax' step earlier in the test had clicked before the tax section loaded. The real problem was a missing wait many lines above the failing line.

questions.question: How do you reduce bugs in the automation scripts you write?
questions.answer: Automation code is software, so it needs the same quality practices as application code. (1) Understand the test case fully and perform it manually before automating it. (2) Follow the framework's standards: Page Object Model, naming conventions and small single-purpose methods, and reuse the common wrappers for click, type and wait rather than writing raw Selenium calls. (3) Use explicit waits and stable locators; never use fixed sleeps or absolute XPath. (4) Write meaningful assertions with clear messages. A test with no assertion, or a weak one, cannot fail and gives false confidence. (5) Make every test independent, with its own data and cleanup. (6) Prove the test can fail: change the expected value or the application state on purpose and confirm the test turns red. A test that passes whatever happens is a defect. (7) Run the test several times locally, then in the CI configuration (headless, parallel), before merging. (8) Have every change peer-reviewed through a pull request. (9) Use static analysis tools such as SonarLint, and handle exceptions properly without empty catch blocks. (10) Keep tests under version control, refactor regularly and remove duplication. (11) Add logging and screenshots so that any failure can be diagnosed quickly.
questions.realTimeExample: During review, a colleague noticed a new test asserting 'Assert.assertTrue(true)' after a try/catch that swallowed exceptions, so it could never fail. It was rewritten to assert the order status directly, and immediately exposed that the order was not being created for one payment type.

questions.question: How do you identify and fix memory leaks in automation tests?
questions.answer: In automation, a memory leak means resources that are created by the tests and never released, so memory use grows as the run continues until the machine slows down or fails with OutOfMemoryError. Common causes: (1) browsers and driver processes that are never closed, because driver.quit() is missing, is skipped when a test fails, or close() was used instead of quit(), leaving chromedriver and browser processes behind; (2) ThreadLocal values that are never removed, which keeps drivers and objects alive in pooled threads; (3) static collections, such as a static list or map of results, screenshots or page objects, that grow for the whole run; (4) unclosed resources such as file streams, Excel workbooks, database connections and HTTP clients; (5) large objects held in memory, for example every screenshot kept as a Base64 string in the report object, or very large data files loaded whole. How to identify: watch the operating system's process list for leftover browser and driver processes after a run; monitor the JVM heap with VisualVM, JConsole or Java Flight Recorder and look for memory that keeps rising and does not fall after garbage collection; take a heap dump and analyse it with Eclipse MAT to see which objects hold the memory; and notice symptoms such as tests slowing down late in a long run or agents needing restarts. Fixes: quit the driver in @AfterMethod(alwaysRun = true) and call remove() on the ThreadLocal; use try-with-resources for streams, workbooks and connections; avoid static collections or clear them; save screenshots to disk and link them; process big files as streams; and add a pipeline step that kills leftover driver processes as a safety net.
questions.realTimeExample: A Jenkins agent became slow every few days and builds started timing out. The process list showed over 200 leftover chromedriver processes. Tests that failed in @BeforeMethod never reached the quit() call. Moving quit() into @AfterMethod(alwaysRun = true) with a null check stopped the leak.

questions.question: How do you scale automation as the application and team grow?
questions.answer: Scaling has four sides: tests, execution, people and process. Tests and architecture: keep a modular framework, organised by application module, with shared core code separated from module-specific pages and tests; in larger organisations publish the core as a versioned library used by several teams. Follow the test pyramid so that growth happens mostly in fast API and component tests, with a limited number of end-to-end UI tests. Keep tests independent with their own data so the suite can be run in any order and in parallel. Execution: run in parallel on a Grid, containers or a cloud provider that scales on demand; split the suite into shards across CI machines; and run in layers, smoke on every commit, impacted modules on pull requests and full regression nightly, so feedback time does not grow with the suite. People: coding standards, a contribution guide, templates and onboarding documentation; mandatory code review; clear ownership of each module's tests; and shared knowledge sessions. Process and health: tests run in CI as a quality gate; track metrics such as pass rate, flaky rate, execution time and failure causes; quarantine and fix flaky tests quickly; regularly remove obsolete and duplicate tests; and keep dependencies and browsers updated. The aim is that adding the next thousand tests or the next five engineers does not make the suite slower, less reliable or harder to understand.
questions.realTimeExample: As a product grew from one team to six, the single automation repository became slow and full of merge conflicts. The common driver, wait and reporting code was extracted into a shared library, each team took ownership of its module's tests, and the pipeline was split into parallel shards. Feedback time stayed under 30 minutes while the suite tripled in size.

questions.question: How do you do code review for test scripts, and what pull-request guidelines would you set for a test repository?
questions.answer: Review test code as seriously as application code, with attention to what makes tests trustworthy. What I check: (1) Correctness of the test: does it verify the requirement, are the assertions meaningful, and can the test fail? (2) Design: Page Object Model followed, no locators or raw driver calls in tests, existing utilities reused, no duplication. (3) Stability: explicit waits, no Thread.sleep, stable locators, no dependency on other tests or on execution order. (4) Data: nothing hard-coded, unique data, cleanup present, no credentials or secrets in the code. (5) Readability: clear names for tests and methods, small methods, comments only where needed. (6) Parallel safety: no shared static state. (7) Error handling: no empty catch blocks. (8) Proper groups or tags, and logging. Pull-request guidelines: keep pull requests small and focused on one purpose; use a descriptive title with the story or ticket number; include a description of what was added and evidence that the tests pass, such as a CI run link; the pipeline must be green, including compilation, static analysis and the new tests run several times; at least one reviewer must approve before merge; no direct commits to the main branch; resolve all review comments; follow the branch naming convention; and update documentation or test data with the code. Give feedback politely and specifically, explain the reason, and automate style checks so reviewers can concentrate on logic.
questions.realTimeExample: A pull request added 12 tests. The review found three Thread.sleep(5000) calls, a hard-coded QA URL and two tests sharing one user. The author replaced the sleeps with waits, moved the URL to configuration and generated unique users. The CI job then ran the new tests five times without a failure before the merge.

questions.question: How do you define automation ROI metrics and report progress to leadership?
questions.answer: ROI (return on investment) compares what automation saves with what it costs. A simple formula is ROI = (savings - investment) / investment. Savings come mainly from manual effort avoided: manual execution time per cycle, multiplied by the number of cycles, multiplied by the hourly cost. Investment includes the effort to build the framework and scripts, ongoing maintenance, tools, licences and infrastructure. Because automation has a high initial cost, also show the break-even point: the number of runs after which savings exceed the investment. Time saved is not the whole value, so report these as well. Coverage: percentage of regression cases automated and coverage of critical flows. Speed: regression cycle time before and after, and how quickly feedback reaches developers. Quality: defects found by automation, especially before release, and the trend of defects escaping to production. Reliability: pass rate and flaky-test rate, since unreliable automation has negative value. Cost of upkeep: maintenance effort as a share of total effort. Release impact: how often the team can release. Reporting to leadership: use a one-page dashboard with trends over time rather than raw counts; express results in business terms such as days saved per release, faster time to market and risk reduced; state the current status, the next goal and what is blocking progress; and be honest about limits, for example that the number of automated tests is not a measure of quality on its own.
questions.realTimeExample: Manual regression took 5 testers 4 days, 160 hours, per release, with two releases a month. Automation cost 1,200 hours to build and needs 20 hours of maintenance a month. It saves about 300 hours a month, so it broke even in roughly the fifth month. The leadership slide showed regression time falling from 4 days to 3 hours and releases moving from monthly to fortnightly.

questions.question: How do you verify that a confirmation email was sent after user registration?
questions.answer: Do not automate a real webmail interface such as Gmail in the browser: it is slow, blocks automation and has its own security checks. Use one of these approaches. (1) An email testing service with an API, such as Mailosaur, Mailtrap or MailSlurp. Each test registers with a unique address on the test domain, then polls the service's API until the message arrives, and asserts the recipient, subject, body text and links. (2) A local fake SMTP server in the test environment, such as MailHog or MailPit. The application sends all email to it and the test reads the messages through its REST API. (3) Reading a real mailbox by protocol, IMAP with the Jakarta Mail library or the Gmail API, searching for the message by recipient and subject. (4) Checking the back end: query the application's email log or outbox table, or the email provider's API, to confirm the message was queued and sent. This proves sending but not the content the user sees. Good practice in every case: use a unique email address per test so messages cannot be confused in parallel runs; wait by polling with a timeout, because delivery takes a few seconds; assert the important content, not only that an email exists; extract the confirmation link from the body and open it with Selenium to complete the flow; and clean up the test mailbox.
questions.realTimeExample: A registration test creates the address reg_8f3a2c@test-inbox.example, submits the form, polls the email service for up to 60 seconds, asserts the subject 'Confirm your account', extracts the verification link with a regular expression, opens it in the browser and asserts that the account status becomes 'Verified'.
buzzWords: Email Testing Service or Fake SMTP

questions.question: How do you configure visual comparison checks for dynamic dashboard charts?
questions.answer: Visual testing compares a screenshot with an approved baseline image and reports the differences. Charts are difficult because their content changes with live data and they are animated, so the task is to remove or control everything that varies. (1) Make the data fixed: load the dashboard with a known data set, by seeding the test database or by mocking the API response that feeds the chart, so the chart is identical on every run. (2) Freeze time-based content: use a fixed date range, and mock or hide 'last updated' timestamps. (3) Disable animations and wait until the chart has finished rendering before capturing, for example by injecting CSS that turns off transitions and waiting for the chart's final element. (4) Capture the chart element, not the whole page, so unrelated areas cannot cause differences. (5) Fix the rendering environment: same browser and version, window size, device scale factor and fonts, ideally by running in a Docker container, because rendering differs between machines. (6) Set a tolerance: allow a small percentage of pixel difference to absorb anti-aliasing, and use ignore regions or masks for areas that are truly dynamic. (7) Manage baselines: store them in version control or the tool's server, review and approve changes deliberately, and keep separate baselines per browser and resolution. Tools: Applitools Eyes with AI-based comparison and layout or ignore regions, Percy, AShot or a pixel-comparison library for Selenium, and Playwright's built-in screenshot assertions. Visual checks complement functional checks; the numbers behind the chart should still be verified through the API or the DOM.
questions.realTimeExample: A revenue dashboard test mocks the chart API to return a fixed twelve-month data set, disables animations, waits for the last bar to render and compares a screenshot of the chart element with the baseline at a 0.5 percent tolerance. It caught a release where the legend colours for two series had been swapped, which no functional assertion covered.

questions.question: How do you integrate Axe-core accessibility checks into automation?
questions.answer: Axe-core is an open-source accessibility testing engine from Deque. It scans a page against rules based on the WCAG standards and reports violations such as missing image alt text, form fields without labels, low colour contrast and incorrect ARIA attributes. For Selenium with Java, add the Deque axe-core Selenium dependency. In a test, open the page and bring it to the state you want to check, then run new AxeBuilder().analyze(driver). It injects the axe script into the page and returns a Results object. getViolations() gives the list of violated rules, each with an id, an impact level (minor, moderate, serious or critical), a description, a help URL and the affected elements. Assert that the list is empty, or fail only on serious and critical violations. Options: withTags() limits the scan to chosen standards such as 'wcag2a' and 'wcag2aa'; include() and exclude() limit it to part of the page; and disableRules() turns off a rule temporarily for a known issue. Integration: put the scan in a helper and call it at important points in existing UI tests, after the page is loaded and again after opening dialogs or menus; attach the violations to the report; and run it in CI. Introduce it gradually, starting by failing only on critical issues. State the limit: automated tools find only a portion of accessibility problems, roughly a third to a half, so manual checks with keyboard navigation and a screen reader are still needed.
questions.realTimeExample: After adding an axe scan to the login and checkout tests, the pipeline reported that the 'Pay' icon button had no accessible name and that the error text failed the contrast requirement. Both were fixed before release, and the checks now stop such issues returning.

questions.question: How would you compare two Excel files with 1 million records each and report the differences efficiently?
questions.answer: This is a data-processing problem, not a browser one, and the two risks are memory and time. (1) Do not load the files with the normal Apache POI classes (XSSFWorkbook), which hold the whole workbook in memory and will run out of memory at this size. Read them as a stream, row by row, using POI's event (SAX) API or a streaming reader library, or convert both files to CSV first and read them line by line. (2) Do not compare every row with every other row; that is a million times a million comparisons. Compare by key. Identify the unique key column, such as an id. Read the first file and store each key with a hash of the rest of the row in a HashMap. Then stream the second file: for each row look up the key. If it is absent, the row exists only in the second file. If present, compare the hashes: different means a modified row. Remove matched keys as you go; whatever is left in the map at the end exists only in the first file. This needs one pass per file and constant-time lookups. Storing a hash instead of the full row keeps memory low. (3) Alternatives: load both files into database tables and find differences with SQL (EXCEPT or MINUS, or a full outer join on the key), which is simple and fast for very large data; or sort both files by key and walk through them together. (4) Reporting: write the differences to a CSV or Excel report as you find them, with the key, the type of difference (missing in A, missing in B, changed) and the changed columns, plus a summary of counts. (5) Before the detailed comparison, compare cheap things first: row counts, column headers and file checksums; identical checksums mean no further work.
questions.realTimeExample: After a data migration, the export from the old system and the new system each had 1.1 million customer rows. The comparison streamed both files, used customer id as the key and reported 37 changed rows and 4 missing rows in about a minute, with the differing columns listed, which pointed to a date-format conversion defect.
questions.expectedOutput:
CHANGED   : key 2 -> 2,Ravi,Mumbai
ONLY IN B : 4,John,Goa
ONLY IN A : key 3
Summary: changed=1, onlyInA=1, onlyInB=1
buzzWords: Compare by Key with a HashMap

questions.question: How did you integrate AWS into your project, and what reporting mechanism did you use?
questions.answer: Describe only the services you have actually used. The common ways an automation project uses AWS are these. (1) Execution infrastructure: Jenkins agents or a Selenium Grid running on EC2 instances, or Grid nodes running as Docker containers on ECS or EKS so they scale up for a run and down afterwards. AWS CodeBuild and CodePipeline can run the Maven test command as a pipeline stage instead of Jenkins. (2) Browser and device cloud: AWS Device Farm offers a desktop browser testing grid. The test asks Device Farm for a temporary Grid URL through the AWS SDK and passes it to RemoteWebDriver; it also provides real mobile devices for Appium. (3) Storage of results: reports, screenshots, logs and videos are uploaded to an S3 bucket at the end of the run, either with the AWS CLI in the pipeline or with the SDK, and the report can be served as a static site from S3 for the team to open by link. (4) Secrets: credentials and API keys are read from AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, not from files in Git. (5) Monitoring and notification: logs and metrics go to CloudWatch, and SNS or a Lambda function sends the run summary to email or a chat channel. (6) Test data and environments: the application under test and its database (RDS) run in AWS, and tests may read or seed data there. Reporting mechanism: the framework generates an Extent or Allure HTML report; the pipeline publishes it, to Jenkins and to S3, and sends a notification with the pass and fail counts and the report link.
questions.realTimeExample: "Our Jenkins ran on EC2 and started Selenium Grid nodes as containers for each run. After the tests, the pipeline uploaded the Allure report and failure screenshots to an S3 bucket in a folder named by build number, and a notification with the summary and the report link was sent to the team channel. Database passwords came from Secrets Manager."
